Madam Speaker, I have two petitions to present this morning.
The first one, signed by Canadians from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec, calls upon Parliament to support the NDP plan to restore VIA Rail services which were cut on January 15, 1990, to maintain and where appropriate upgrade remote services on which many Canadians rely, provide a legislative mandate for VIA Rail and make available to VIA the resources which it needs to become a modem passenger rail system in a class with those throughout the rest of the western world.

Madam Speaker, I have been asked by a number of citizens of my community of Thunder Bay to table a petition which expresses concern about the situation in eastern Europe, particularly in the Baltic States. It calls upon Parliament to allocate and activate credits for feed grain to Lithuania and the neighbouring Baltic states.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to present a petition today pursuant to Standing Order 36 in regard to the situation in East Timor.
Indonesia has occupied East Timor since 1975 in contravention of international law. This military occupation has caused death of hundreds of thousands of East Timorese men, women, and children.
Canada has shown its world-wide support in the work of the United Nations and has recently sent armed forces to aid Kuwait in the removal of an aggressor state.
Constituents from my riding and throughout British Columbia ask that the Canadian government work toward the elimination of the Indonesian military occupation of East Timor and the genocide of East Timorese people.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today marks an important milestone on a journey which began several years ago. The legislation before us today is a major work of reform, the reform of the legislation governing Canada's financial institutions.
We first want to indicate that we are fully aware of the contributions made by former Ministers of Finance and the finance committee of this House and the other place. We also want to pay tribute to the contributions made by countless individuals and groups, both in the industries affected directly and among the general public.
This particular stage of financial institutions reform includes four bills. The first of these was Bill C-4, which has already been considered in committee and which applied the principles of reform to the federally chartered trust and loan companies. The other three bills are C-19, which applies these principles to the chartered banks; C-28, which applied them to federally chartered insurance companies; and C-34, which applies them to federally regulated financial co-operatives.
In each case, the basic approach taken in the bill is the same. There are differences between the bills, however, because each applies the underlying principles of reform to a different type of institution. Shortly I want to look at the ways in which reform has been applied to each of these three bills which are awaiting second reading. Before I do this, however, I want to review the more general aspects of our reform which apply to all three pieces of legislation.
September 26, 1991

One of the most important points is that this process of reform will bring all federal legislation governing financial institutions into harmony to a degree we have not previously experienced; a major achievement and one of which this government is proud.
The goals of reform are clear and easy to understand. They are: to enhance protection for depositors and policy holders; to benefit consumers by increasing competition and the spectrum of services offered by financial institutions; to strengthen the ability of our financial institutions to compete at home and abroad; and to lay the groundwork for discussions with the provinces about harmonization, because jurisdiction in the general field of financial institutions is a shared one.
These goals, Madam Speaker, are important and I am pleased that we have been able to embody them in legislative and regulatory reform.
I know that members of the House are familiar with the general outlines of the proposals. We have dealt with them already in Bill C-4 and its predecessor. But I do want to speak specifically about certain issues.
The first of these is the problem of self-dealing. Tougher rules will be implemented; the self-policing role of directors and auditors will be made more effective through mandated roles and responsibilities; the superintendent of financial institutions will have increased powers to require information that will enable problems to be anticipated; and the superintendent is therefore being given new access which has not previously been available.
Second, consumers will find shopping for financial services more convenient and will benefit from a wider choice of financial products since banks, trust and loan companies and insurance companies will be allowed to compete more directly with each other. By opening new avenues for growth of our financial institutions, the new provisions will strengthen the ability of these institutions to meet the new challenge that has evolved in the global marketplace.
Financial institutions will be able to diversify by owning institutions operating in other segments of the industry. For example, banks will be allowed to own trust companies and insurance companies; and insurance companies will be able to own other financial institu-
Govemment Orders
tions. By virtue of their wide ownership, mutual insurance companies will be able to own chartered banks. Significant changes in the ownership of financial institutions will be subject to approval by the Minister of Finance, who will take account of whether transfers are in the best interests of the Canadian financial system.
Together, these proposals set out a framework for fair competition that will allow all institutions to have good opportunities for participation in financial sector activities. These bills and their regulations cover a very wide range of changes because of the size and the importance of the financial sector and the wide range of institutions and situations which have to be covered. After all, looking at the sectors as a whole, there are more than 3,000 Canadian financial institutions with assets of some $900 billion. Of the 25 largest institutions with total assets of $760 billion, 23 are chartered and regulated federally.
But it is not just the sheer size of the sector which gives it importance.
We must not forget that the health of these institutions is key to the vitality and strength of our economy as well as to our security and the security of savers and investors.
The activities of these institutions affect our mortgages and our purchases of goods and services. The financial sector shelters and invests savings and makes available investment needed for new and expanded industries.
I believe these institutions will operate more effectively and competitively and will meet the needs of Canadians more efficiently as a result of reforms we have put forward. We have recognized the importance of financial institutions in developing a legislative and a regulatory approach that protects the public while encouraging and not inhibiting innovation and competition. We have done this while also recognizing the competing interests within the financial community itself, and while we have sought as wide an agreement as possible not all interests could be completely reconciled. In such cases, we have looked to find a reasonable balance.
I want to go over the particular provisions of Bill C-19, Bill C-28 and Bill C-34 which are unique to each bill.

Government Orders
Bill C-19, which applies to the chartered banks, is very similar to its predecessor, Bill C-95 from the previous session. There have been some relatively small modifications. I want to indicate what the specific changes are.
First, because it is based on Bill C-4, this bill recognizes and incorporates amendments made in committee to Bill C-83, the bill of the previous session relating to trust and loan companies.
Second, a number of changes affecting only banks have been made as a result of comments received since Bill C-95 was tabled.
Third, this bill contains new wording for the section which restricts the retailing of insurance by banks. This section was section 4.17 in the previous bill and is now section 4.16. The proposed new wording sets out clearly the intent of the government's policy. This has been done to meet concerns that the corresponding section of Bill C-4 relating to trust and loan companies on which the previous wording was modelled, does not constitute a clear and certain statement of the intentions to restrict deposit taking institutions from engaging in retailing insurance.
I should add that revised draft regulations issued with Bill C-19 reflect these changes as well as comments and submissions on previously issued draft regulations relating to retailing of insurance.
This means that the banks and the trust and loan companies will be restricted from retailing most insurance products in their branches. This ensures that insurance will continue to be sold by qualified licensed insurance brokers and agents working independently from any deposit taking institution.
Our general approach to the question of ownership of financial institutions has been applied to the special needs of the chartered banks. We have maintained the principle of wide ownership for schedule 1 banks, including the six largest Canadian banks. This ensures that no one person or group of associated persons can own more than 10 per cent of any class of bank shares.
The second bill, Bill C-28, affects insurance companies. In addition to the ownership provisions to which I have already referred, certain elements of the reform are tailored to meet the needs of these institutions. There will be enhanced powers given to insurance companies to make consumer and commercial loans.
In addition, this legislation recognizes the important place of mutual companies within the system. These companies are granted new powers to raise capital through the issuance of debt and preferred shares.
Finally, the legislation recognizes the position of participating policy holders and establishes new rules for communicating with them and seeking their approval for fundamental changes.
Bill C-34 applies the general principles to a third part of the sector, federally regulated financial co-operatives. To an even greater extent than the other parts of the sector, these institutions operate under shared jurisdiction with the provinces.
Currently, one federal association is governed by the act while six registered centrals are governed by both the federal act and legislation of their provinces. Local credit unions continue to be incorporated provincially and are governed solely by provincial legislation.
This legislation grants associations of power to provide a range of services comparable to those that may be provided by trust and loan companies under Bill C-4. A key difference is that associations continue to be restricted to providing their services primarily to their members.
The new legislation permits associations to provide services in the fulfilment of the trade association function which they service with respect to other co-operative institutions.
In adapting the investment rule set out in Bill C-4 to the particular situation of federally regulated financial co-operatives, this legislation takes into account the important liquidity function served by the associations.
Finally, this bill will increase the access of federal associations to capital by permitting them to issue preferred shares to non-members. These shares will be restricted from carrying full voting rights to ensure that control of associations remains within the co-operative system.
Returning to the general outline of our policy, I want to reiterate that our proposals represent a balancing of individual, national, international, federal, provincial, commercial and prudential concerns.
The proposals in this package serve the public interest very well. They will strengthen the financial institution sector and will permit our financial institutions to grow and prosper and contribute to the economic vitality of Canada.
September 26, 1991

I ask all hon. members to work together with the government to expedite consideration of these bills in this package.

Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to participate in second reading this morning on Bill C-19, the new Bank Act, and Bill C-28, the new insurance act. My colleague from Moncton will be discussing the co-operative act on behalf of my party.
I want to make it very clear at the beginning that the Liberal Party of Canada supports in principle this new legislation. The banking and the insurance industries have been waiting a long while for this new legislation. While our party has some concerns about both bills, we will seek to have those concerns addressed when the bills get to committee.
The current insurance legislation is already decades old and the Bank Act is more than a decade. Both are badly in need of modernization, although the insurance act is more outdated and this government has been dragging its feet for six years on financial sector reform ever since it was elected.
The government's reform process started in 1985 with the green paper. A year later it was followed by a blue paper, and last September the government released the white paper on financial reform. All in all, six years have passed since the first green paper was released. The legislation we are debating this morning is certainly long overdue.
When the government proposed in this new legislation, in the new Bank Act, that this legislation we are dealing with today would be reviewed five years after it comes into force, my party suggested that the review would be better three years after it comes into force.
We argued that by 1997 it will be 12 years after the publication of the green paper which started the whole process and seven years after the first financial reform bill was introduced into the House of Commons.
Twelve years is a long time in a fast moving industry such as financial services. The government members on
Government Orders
the committee obviously felt differently about our proposal as they defeated our amendment.
For too long this government has been holding back federally regulated Canadian financial institutions with outdated legislation. Our financial institutions must be given the new powers they need to compete in the new global business environment. We must also ensure that our consumers are well served and that the strength of the Canadian financial sector is not only protected but enhanced. This is why our party is supporting this legislation in principle.
In addition to helping our financial institutions compete, another major objective of reform is to protect depositors. Here again the government's slowness in this whole area may have been damaging.
The government's new reform package gives the Superintendent of Financial Institutions more powers than ever before, powers such as the setting of accounting standards, the inspection of the books of the parent of a financial institution.
If this legislation had been passed it might have made a difference with Standard Trust. I questioned the Superintendent of Financial Institutions about this at the finance meeting on November 28. At that time I asked the superintendent if he felt that he had been hindered by inadequate legislation in dealing with Standard Trust. I want to read his reply directly from Hansard:
It is very difficult for me to go beyond that with respect to this particular company because, as I said, pretty well everything else we have done here, as with all of the companies, is confidential.
To stand back from this, however, there are a number of things contained in this bill that might, and I say "might", have made a difference to this or other situations in which there are or might be developing difficulties.
The first is the provision I referred to that gives us a lot more leverage on accounting policies. That might have made a difference.
The second is the provision that gives us access to information to parent companies and related companies. It is possible that might have made a difference.
The third is the establishment of business conduct review committees of directors to review any related party transactions, and finally of course there is the whole regime of prohibitions and bans of related party transactions. All of these might have made a difference. I do not know.

September 26, 1991
Government Orders
No one knows for sure but the 150,000 Standard Trust depositors whose accounts were frozen on April 18 probably wish that the government had kept its promise and put those new accounting rules in place a few years ago.
Another example concerns the new insurance legislation. Under Bill C-28 the insurance companies, until that becomes law, will continue to have to make complex legal arrangements to accomplish things which the old act allows but makes very difficult.
Those extra legal bills are being charged to and paid for by the consumer or policy holders in the way of higher premiums.
With this new legislation that we have before us this morning insurance companies will be allowed to act more freely, and this should mean lower legal bills.
Just to give a simple example as to how outdated this legislation is, under the current act the board of directors of an insurance company must approve all employees' salaries who earn more than $40,000. Obviously that rule was established decades ago when in those days we probably had only two or three top executives earning over $40,000. Now that is a very simple example of how outdated this government has allowed Canada's insurance legislation to become.
I think those examples illustrate very well why the government must move as quickly as possible to improve financial sector legislation.
This morning I want to discuss both Bill C-19 and Bill C-28 in some detail. As I mentioned earlier, my colleague from Moncton will deal with the Co-operative Act on behalf of my party. Together these two acts, the Bank Act and the insurance act, comprise about 1,400 sections, well over 800 pages. Each bill is over an inch thick. This morning I want to try and highlight a few of the most important sections of each bill and some of the issues that they raise.
I will begin by discussing the sections that the two bills have in common and there are many.
The first major item is natural person powers. In other words, both insurance companies and banks will be able to do anything that is not clearly prohibited by legislation. Under the current legislation insurance companies can only do what is clearly permitted by their legislation. So that in itself is a big change.
Some of the other common elements in the banking and insurance company legislation are measures to protect the soundness of this legislation. Of course the main reason for having factors like this in these two bills is to protect the savings of the Canadian consumers. We do not want what has happened in the United States to happen here. We want to be sure, positively certain, that our depositors are protected.
In this legislation both types of institutions, banks and insurance companies, will be required to ensure that one-third of their board of directors is unaffiliated with the company. For example, if an insurance company has 21 directors sitting on a board, at least seven cannot be among other things an employee of the company, an officer of the company, someone who has a substantial investment in the company, or someone whose company does more than 10 per cent of his or her business with the insurance company.
By doing this the government of course is trying to ensure some degree of independence on the board, and we agree with that.
An insurance company or a bank will also need to have in place proper procedures for dealing with conflict of interest.
They will have to establish two committees: an audit committee and a conduct review committee. Of course these committees again will help to protect depositors and consumers.
The audit committee is there to review any problems raised by the auditor's report and the conduct review committee will review possible self-dealing situations.
Self-dealing might exist, for example, where a director of a company has influence over the company in such a way that it would benefit him personally.
One item that we in the Liberal Party were pleased to see in both bills was a consumer complaint section. This section is actually based on a Liberal amendment to the Trust and Loan Companies Act which the finance committee passed in March.
As I said, this was an amendment that we proposed in the finance committee to the trust and loan legislation. We are extremely pleased that the government has now included this in the Bank Act and the Insurance Act. What that does is ensure the legal right of customers to complain about a problem they have with the bank,
September 26, 1991

insurance company or other financial institutions. They can complain about service charges or other concerns that they have.
First of all, they take their complaint to the institution itself. If it is not resolved there then they can go directly to the Superintendent of Financial Institutions. They have the legal right to do so. For example, the bank forecloses on a loan to a farmer. The farmer thinks the bank's action was unjust. He now has the legal right to see the bank's consumer complaints officer. If together the officer and the farmer cannot resolve the problem, the farmer could take his complaint right to the top, to the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions.
The superintendent now has to include in his annual report a section on these complaints. The number and types of complaints received by the superintendent's office will be detailed in this section, as well as a general description of how those complaints were resolved.
Certainly we on this side of the House hope that by legally requiring banks and other financial institutions to have complaint procedures in place we can ensure that customers who do have complaints will be better served.
There are some other elements of the insurance legislation that are also found in the banking bill, such as the new ownership rules. Insurance companies will now be able to own financial institutions such as schedule banks and trust companies. Of course, banks will be able to own insurance companies and trust companies. Both will also be able to own corporations that are in the financial services family such as the financial leasing companies and information processing companies.
The legislation limits the flexibility of insurance companies and banks to invest in these other corporations I have just mentioned. If these financial institutions do not wish to own at least 51 per cent, then they will not be allowed to own more than 10 per cent. For example, they cannot invest in 30 per cent of the company. It has to be 10 per cent or 51 per cent.
It seems that the government's goal here is to reduce the risk of a bank getting into a new kind of business that it is not familiar with and not able to control. The banks
Government Orders
and the insurance companies argue that these new rules will prevent them from getting into joint ventures and getting into a business with a major partner or a partner who has the expertise to help them in running the company. Again, this is something that we certainly want to look at in committee.
There are many common elements to the two bills, but there are obviously some major elements in the new acts which are unique to the insurance and the banking industry. I want to start with the insurance bill.
Insurance companies will soon have full commercial and consumer lending powers. In other words, they will be able to make loans to the general public, not only to their policy holders.
Those insurance policy holders will also get new rights under the new act. Tliey will be treated more like shareholders of a corporation. They will receive regular notification of their rights as policy holders and those who express an interest will receive notice of company board meetings.
Policy holders will also have the right, where the numbers are sufficient, to make proposals to the board of directors.
In a very important change in this legislation, mutual insurance companies-and I am talking here about companies that are owned by their policyholders-will get the right to issue preferred shares and thereby raise much needed capital.
The government has also released a proposal that would allow mutual companies to demutualize or accept shareholders as well as policyholders. This alternative method of raising capital raises many issues, such as how would the policyholders rank as compared to the shareholders? There are several questions around this whole issue that certainly will have to be addressed in committee.
Briefly those are some of the major elements of the new Insurance Act. While we understand that the insurance industry is generally quite pleased with this new legislation, we have yet to hear from various interest groups.

September 26, 1991
Government Orders
There is one group that we have heard from, the Canadian Bankers' Association. It has some concerns about Bill C-28, respecting the insurance act. It feels that it does not effectively restrict insurance companies from accepting deposits or offering cheque writing services. As we know, banks are prohibited under this legislation from selling insurance and they want insurance companies to keep out of the banking business.
The Canadian Bankers' Association also wants insurance companies to face the same requirements as banks and trust companies in terms of disclosure of service charges, networking arrangements and turning over unclaimed accounts to the government.
They have some other concerns as well, all of which we will be addressing in committee.
I would like to turn now to the main sections of the new Bank Act. One of the main provisions in the new Bank Act would continue to prohibit banks from moving any further into the insurance market.
We in the Liberal Party have heard arguments for and against, and I want to take a few minutes this morning to talk about some of these arguments from both sides of the issue.
We have been told that if banks could sell insurance, it would be cheaper and it would be more convenient for consumers.
We were told that there would be no risk of tied selling. What I mean by tied selling is that a bank would try to pressure a customer into buying insurance from the bank by threatening them that they would deny a mortgage.
We were told that around the world, and even here in Canada, deposit-taking institutions sell insurance with no consumer problems and they sell at very competitive prices.
We have also heard many reasons on the other side of this issue; why banks should not receive broad insurance powers. First of all, we were told that there is no evidence that banks could sell life insurance, the main product they want to sell, any more cheaply than insurance companies over the long term. It is argued that, yes, in the short term banks may undercut the prices of insurance companies in order to gain the market share and consumers would benefit in the short term. But in the long term, the argument goes, it is still
far from certain that banks would offer life insurance at super competitive prices.
For example, in 1989, there was a study done by the Public Interest Research Centre that claimed consumers could save a lot of money if banks could sell insurance. However, that study has been discredited by a 1991 study done by Eckler and Partners.
We have also heard the argument to give the banks broad insurance powers would be unfair because of the size of the banks. With assets of $126 billion, one bank, the Royal Bank, is larger than the entire insurance industry put together. There are six major banks involved. Together, the six big banks account for 90 per cent of the $584 billion in Canadian banking assets.
So it is argued that there is a very real possibility of unequal competition.
It has been suggested also that it is possible that there could be a very short but intense battle between the huge chartered banks and the much smaller life insurance companies which could lead to massive dislocations in the insurance industry.
The insurance industry in Canada comprises 170 companies and 20,000 agents, so a lot of Canadians could lose their jobs and a very successful insurance industry that serves rural and urban Canadians could be permanently damaged by such a battle between unequals.
There is also some evidence to suggest that tied selling, which I described earlier, could be a problem. There was a survey done by the Canadian Life Health Insurance Association. They did a study on the insurance regulators. This study was done in 1990. They wrote to and received letters from 22 United States' insurance regulators. The response confirmed that many states do not permit banks to enter the insurance business and those that do have significant concerns about the coercion and misuse of customer information.
That does not necessarily mean that we might have the same problem here in Canada, but it is certainly a factor which we have to consider when looking at this issue. One of the areas which is certainly related to insurance is the question of banks selling life annuities. Life annuities are a retirement product now only sold by insurance companies. The banks want a share of the market. They argue that as the Canadian population ages, more and more of their customers will require life annuities and they should be able to buy them from their banks.
September 26, 1991

The banks argue that Canadians will benefit if they enter the life annuity market. They feel that life annuities are crucial to any retirement plan. With their superior distribution system, the banks say it will be easier for Canadians to prepare for retirement. On the other hand, the insurance companies argue that life annuities should be part of the over-all ban on banks selling insurance.
This is another area that we certainly want to explore further in committee. As you can see, we have had some very conflicting views to date on whether banks should be able to sell insurance. Certainly, we are considering our position in the Liberal Party very carefully because there is a lot at stake.
The next section that I want to deal with involves consumers. That is whether banks and trust companies should be able to enter the auto leasing business. Again, we have heard arguments on both sides of the issue. We have heard that consumers would get lower prices, that it would be more convenient if people could lease a car through a bank rather than an auto dealer.
There are concerns again on the other side of this issue, that it might be unfair competition. A bank with a loan to a car dealer would have detailed information on that car dealer. Armed with that information on their main competitor, a bank could undercut the car dealer long enough to drive him out of business. Here again, we have to consider very carefully our position on this issue.
Leaving consumer issues and turning to international matters for a moment, the new Bank Act changes the rules for foreign banks setting up in Canada. The legislation now says in effect to qualify for a foreign Schedule 2 bank licence, an applicant must prove to the government it is a bank in its home country.
Given that definition, certainly we in the Liberal Party and others were quite surprised, extremely surprised when American Express was granted a foreign bank licence. AMEX is clearly not a bank in the United States as the spirit of the law and the government's own guidelines required. The government, however, said AMEX met its legal definition of a bank.
It is also curious that AMEX, a major supporter of the free trade agreement, received its licence on November
Government Orders
21, 1988. All members of this House remember what day that was. Of course, it was election day. That is when AMEX received its licence.
This certainly raises serious questions about whether the government was playing politics with the Canadian financial sector.
Whatever the case, Bill C-19 could set the stage for more AMEXs because the new Bank Act says the government can grant a foreign Schedule 2 bank licence if the applicant is either a bank or it is a widely held financial institution, or is in some way engaged in the financial services business. This section runs counter to the government's September 1990 white paper where it is stated that a foreign applicant had to be either a bank or a regulated financial institution in its home jurisdiction.
The new Bank Act says nothing about being regulated, and this has Canadian banks very worried. They are worried that the new act could open the door to a whole range of unregulated non-bank foreign institutions, including the financial arm of huge American commercial companies like Ford, Chrysler, Sears, IBM and General Electric.
These foreign non-banks do many of the things that our Canadian banks do. They raise money not through deposits, but by taking short-term loans known as commercial paper. This sounds like banking, even though these institutions are unregulated and commercially linked.
They would obviously be regulated if they entered Canada as banks. Allowing such commercially linked companies into Canada raises concerns about fairness to Canadian banks and about the soundness of the Canadian financial institutions. One can therefore legitimately ask whether the government is putting our banks at a disadvantage with this new legislation.
We are also concerned about the degree of discretion that the new Bank Act gives the finance minister in handing out these foreign bank licences. The minister can decide what is a financial institution and what is meant by "widely held".

Government Orders
What this does, of course, is leave the government open to intense lobbying by foreign institutions which maybe should not qualify for a Canadian banking licence and whose presence here in Canada could undermine confidence in the Canadian banking system. As we saw in the case of AMEX, when international politics and banking mix, Canadian financial institutions are often the losers.
All these questions are extremely important and they must be dealt with in committee. The government's changes to the foreign bank role raises the whole issue of international trade and financial services.
As Canadians know, this country is involved in two sets of international trade negotiations: first, with the United States and Mexico, and second, with other GATT countries. GATT of course, stands for General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
While this government has not yet revealed its strategy for these negotiations, it seems very clear that the foreign countries will demand similar treatment to that given Americans under the free trade agreement. We in the Liberal Party want to state once again that the government must not use these trade negotiations to weaken the competitive position of Canadian financial institutions.
I would like to conclude my remarks by briefly summarizing the stand of my party. The Liberal Party supports in principle the government's new Bank Act and insurance act, although we have some major concerns, many of which I have mentioned briefly today. Certainly we look forward to reviewing and addressing these concerns in the finance committee.

Madam Speaker, on a point of order. There have been some discussions and I think you would find unanimous agreement to allow my colleague, the member for Nickel Belt, to speak for 40 minutes on these three bills.
As you would appreciate, if they had been done separately he would have about 60 minutes. He is being very conservative today in the time he wants. You will notice that I did not ask for unlimited time because, as we found out in the past, he can go on at great length.
Madam Speaker, I agree with everything the hon. member said, particularly his last comment. We are happy to accede to the request.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand that there is also agreement on my right. Therefore I will recognize the hon. member for Nickel Belt and he will be allowed his 40 minutes.

Madam Speaker, I will try to stay within the 40 minutes I have been allotted.
These three bills are very complex. I thought long and hard as to how I could take such very complicated and convoluted legislation and put it in a way that people who are listening and watching could understand the complexities, the twisting and the turnings of the operations of the financial institutions of this country.
I thought I should put it in a way that people understood. I said: "Who best could describe things in a way that people could understand but Aesop?" Therefore I have put my opening remarks in the terms of Aesop's Fables.
Is everybody ready? Are we all gathered around? Once upon a time, shortly after 1929, certain animals were put in cages and there were four cages. In cage number one were the rabbits. These rabbits, I would say, are the equivalent of investment brokers. We have rabbits as investment brokers.
In the next cage was put lions, big, king of the beasts, and they are the banks. They were put in their cages and the lock was put on.
In the third cage was put the mongoose. I do not know what the plural of mongoose is. I think it is mongeese or maybe it is mongooses. They were put in the third cage, and they were the insurance companies, and a lock was put on the cage.
In the fourth cage was put the cobra, and the cobra were the trust companies, and the gatekeeper put the lock on the cage. We had the four cages: the rabbits, the lions, the mongoose and cobra. Everybody knows, there they are after 1929. Before 1929 they did terrible things to each other so they were put in the cages.
In 1987 somebody whose begins with t and ends withy, a four letter word, stealthily in the night went and opened the rabbits' cage and the lions' cage. Well, everybody knows that lions eat rabbits. That is what happened. The lions ate up the rabbits; the banks ate up the investment brokers.
September 26, 1991

That reminds me of a limerick:
A smiling young investment broker from Vancouver Went for a ride on a banker.
They came back from the ride with the broker inside And a smile on the face of the banker.
That is what happened. Maybe it was not supposed to happen, but everybody knows that if we put lions and rabbits together, the lions will eat the rabbits. That is what happened.
Here we are today, in 1991, and somebody beginning with a t and ending with ay, a four letter word, in Bill C-19 and Bill C-28 are stealthily going to open the cages separating the cobra, the mongoose and the lion.
We know what will happen. We know what mongoose do to the cobra; it kills them. Then what do the lions do to the mongoose? They are going to eat them. As sure as shooting, we are going to end up, when the dust settles, with a brand new animal.
It will have a lion's head. It will have the body of the cobra, the feet of the rabbit and the teeth of the mongoose. Do you know who it feeds on? Consumers. And who is there to keep this animal with all these attributes, this new creation, this new hybrid, to separate this monster from his feed.
Well, we call in somebody called OSFI. You see him there with his lion tamer's hat and his little whip, and that is all that is between this hybrid monster and consumers.
What I have tried to portray in this little fable is in fact the reality of Bill C-19, Bill C-28, Bill C-4 financial institutions which we previously called Bill C-83. What we are doing with these bills today is that we are opening up the cages. We in this party have always said when you do that, when you collapse the pillars, when you open the cages, what will result is a concentration of economic power.
One morning we will wake up and there are not going to be any Hulk Hogan's wrestling out there. There will just be one huge sumo wrestler, which we have cultivated to go and wrestle globally. That is a danger.
Government Orders
I do not have to remind members of the realities in California where previous deregulation under Ronald Reagan there were many banks and financial institutions in California. If we go there today, it is predominated by two particular banks: the Bank of America and Securities Pacific. There is also a smaller one, First Interstate Bank of California. All of that is going to shake down and, sure as shooting, eventually there is only going to be one bank in California.
We have serious concerns. When you open the cages, you cannot control the animals, and the biggest and the most aggressive one will survive. We have said consistently that we have to keep the pillars in place. There is no problem, as far as we can see, with banks entering into joint venture arrangements to market insurance products. But the minute you allow this feeding frenzy, sure as shooting one morning we are going to wake up and there is only going to be one financial institution, one giant, super financial institution at which all Canadians are going to do their banking and their financial services.
That is not going to be healthy for the marketplace. I am absolutely amazed that a Conservative government that worships so grovelingly at the altar of the marketplace would in fact destroy the marketplace. In fact, the reason they were put in the cages after 1929 was because of their rampant behaviour in 1929. Now we are opening it up. We want a market that can be regulated, because we want it to make sure that it behaves in a socially responsible manner.
The Tories are destroying the market through this monopoly. Historically it shows that to control a monopoly you need another monopoly. Therefore the Tories, quod erat demonstrandum, are for big government. We are going to have to have a monstrosity to control a monopoly.
Look at the bills and the regulations. Everywhere in these bills and regulations you will see: "The minister shall" or "OSFI shall" or "the government shall". It seems to me we ought to be striving for built-in structures that by their very nature regulate the industry.
It seems to me that if you work toward getting those kinds of built-in rules, regulations and structures, then you have a check and a balance: for example, the pillar structure, for example the 10 per cent ownership rule.

Government Orders
There is another concern that this deregulation will allow financial institutions to become so huge, so economically powerful that they will challenge the state. They become in fact major private governments. There are three powers which they are headed to control: the power to create money, the power to control productivity, that is real wealth, and the power to control technology. What we are developing here as I said before is a huge sumo wrestler.
If we listen to the banks, that is all they talk about. They want to go global. What we are going to have is a huge ubiquitous sumo wrestler. He will be everywhere because you will not be able to keep him inside your borders. He will transcend, cross borders. You think we have got a problem with cross-border shopping. Wait until we get cross-border financing because we do not have an international regulator that is going to keep an eye on them. I can just see BCCIs all over the place.
We are really dealing here with the destruction of the national market for the sake of global competition. Banks will be allowed to own insurance companies. The banks cannot retail insurance. I mean, how stupid. We have 7,000 branches. I can just see myself wanting insurance for my car. I do not see absolutely anything wrong with the bank marketing the insurance policies of insurance companies.
If I want insurance for my car, I go down to my bank branch and say to the clerk: "I want insurance. Here is my car, here is the year", and so on. There is no reason he or she could not crank it up on the computer, show me a whole rack of companies and pick the policy and the company that suit my needs. I could also suggest that it would be done at a better rate.
In fact playing this little verbal les jeux de mains, if I may, in trying to say that the banks cannot do it, there is not anything in there that they cannot dipsy-doodle around.
They are going to set up little subsidiaries of insurance companies. They are going to direct market through their credit cards to their customers. They are going to build up a customer base. It is stupid and ridiculous. It does not make any sense. I say you put them back in their
cage and put the lock on it. If they are bankers, they do banking; if they are insurance companies, they do insurance business; if they are trust and loan companies, they do trust and loan business. It is a simple matter.
All we have got to do is look south to what has happened. They wanted to deregulate. Well they deregulated the s and I's all right. They gave them all kinds of powers to go and get involved in real estate operations. This bill has got some real stuff on real estates for financial companies. Have they got stuff. We are going down the road. They are going to be developers too. Do remember what I said about the lion eating the whole gang? All right, we will come to it.
It seems to me that these bills are releasing the dynamism of the Canadian banking system, not to serve the consumer and the public but to predict the system. They eat it up. That is what I think these bills are all about. That is really the principle and the philosophy behind them. Already we are over-banked. We have banks banking. Now you are going to have insurance companies taking deposits. They are selling financial instruments. You have trust companies all over the place. For 26 million people we are over-banked.
I want to tell you very quickly that the feeding frenzy is going to start. It is not good when the end result is the development of a hybrid animal, one only, one super financial institution.
The banks need competition.

They need competition among themselves and that is what we have to make sure they do. They are in the banking business. That is what they are in. Insurance companies are to sell insurance and are not to do banking. That is the principle.
I heard the former chairman of the finance committee expound that theory time and time again: "You are a banker, do banking. You are an insurance company, do insurance".
Would American Express sell insurance?

I will get to American Express, don't worry.
September 26, 1991

We oppose changes to the financial institution structure that concentrate the economic power because we think in that kind of environment the consumers are the losers, the society is the loser. We say banks should not own insurance companies.
We have another concern and it all ties in. I am going to sort of weave this in like a mosaic. Brother, I cannot turn my back on that guy; he has got his sword. Excuse my back, do not get angry.
The other aspect of the bill that concerns me is the question of ownership. For financial institutions, we think one of the best safeguards and one of the best controls is wide ownership. That is why we put into the Bank Act that no group or individual shall own more than 10 per cent of the equity of a bank. That is what we said, and I think it has worked well. The major banks in this country are not the problem in terms of what they do, in terms of kerfuffling; it is the trust companies. Look at what we have done. We have allowed them to be closely held. The 10 per cent rule does not apply to trust companies, and yet in these bills we are giving them all the powers of banks.
They are laughing. They can do all the things. I do not need to remind you that when you start mixing up commercial operations with financial institution operations you are headed for trouble. We just saw Standard Trust. What is a guy who is an expert in the mining business doing in the banking business? That is what we have. How would you react to a Lavelin bank or, dare I say it, a Campeau bank or an Algoma bank? They could have established under these rules. Is that not wonderful?
This is very dangerous. I am not the only one who feels this way. This party is not the only one that feels this way. I want to quote a fellow by the name of E. Gerald Corrigan. He is the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. He appeared before the United States Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs on Thursday, May 3, 1990. This is what he said:
Second, I remain strongly opposed to the merging of banking and commerce and to any arrangements that would even remotely contemplate the ownership and control of bank holding companies or financial services holding companies containing depository institutions by commercial concerns. Here too, on a n earlier occasion, I spelled out before this Committee the reasons for my concerns in this regard, and I have provided an extract of that in earlier testament as Appendix V-1 still look with concern, if not alarm, at the economic, financial -and
Government Orders
perhaps even social-implications of Exxon owing Chase Manhattan, Ford owning Citicorp, or RJR Nabisco owning J. P Morgan. Obviously, those examples draw more than a little hyperbole in order to stress the point. But once that door is opened, there is absolutely no way to anticipate how events will shake out over time. Therefore, and absent that compelling public policy reason I spoke of in my earlier testimony, I would strongly urge that we maintain a strict separation of banking and commerce.
Not only do we have in our banking and financial institution structure non-financial upstream ownership, but we are now heading down the road to downstream non-financial ownership. There are provinces that are actively contemplating that move.
That is a serious concern and it ought to be a serious concern for all members. We gave OSFI improved powers after the banks in the west failed. We gave Mr. Mackenzie additional powers, and yet in spite of that we have had an ineffective supervisory system. Still we have had the case of Standard Trust and we will probably end up with more.
The next concern we have is what I touched on before, and that is the financial institutions playing in the real estate market. Bill C-19 proposes that banks, financial institutions, can be allowed to invest up to 70 per cent of their regulatory capital in real estate holdings, 70 per cent. You are talking here about tens of billions of dollars because you are throwing into it trust companies, insurance companies and banks-tens of billions of dollars.
In the short run they may be bailing out developers in the industry at the moment with this, but think of the potential for conflict of interest. The same people who have developers as their customers will be competing with their customers.
Think of the stranglehold if you applied those tens of billions of dollars to three or four major cities in this country. Think of how you can control the real estate market. Think of the potential of that economic power. I want to bet the bottom dollar that when that happens, you will never see real estate come down in the major cities again, never.
We will have effectively kept the price up. What is this mad dash? It seems to me that the rules at the present time are quite sufficient. What do you think about them pulling in loans prematurely, seizing real estate, and purchasing it themselves?

September 26, 1991
Government Orders
This again is opening the gates. I do not want to mix my metaphors here or as somebody would say open Pandora's box. Where will it end? We have a problem with that.
Another interesting thing is harmonization. These are the kinds of things we should be working on. Presently every province has its own rules for financial institutions. Superimposed on top of that are the federal rules. You have Ontario which gives the "Ontario equals" approach.
These are widely divergent. For example, look in this bill, Bill C-19. There is a 10-50 provision. If a bank wants to purchase a financial entity, it can purchase only less than 10 or more than 50.
The province of Ontario has a basket provision that says: "When you reach a certain level, you cannot go beyond it". So we have the possibility of while a financial institution is trying to maintain the federal rule it violates the provincial rule.
We have tons of examples of conflicts between provincial and federal regulations and rules with respect to financial institutions. We have an example: Scotia McLeod by the way was one of the rabbits. McLeod, Weir, Young is what it used to be called. It was one of the rabbits in the cages.
That was one of the rabbits that the bank or the hon. the Bank of Nova Scotia, ate back in 1987. They have called it ScotiaMcLeod. It is really a subsidiary of the Bank of Nova Scotia.
Under the present law, its investment broker can actually be right inside the golden tower. He has his counter right there in the golden tower in Toronto. He has his plaid jacket. It is called the McLeod tartan so you can recognize him on the floor of the stock exchange. They have team colours and everything. It is amazing. These animals have their own teams and wear little caps with colours on them.
He is allowed to be in the bank. The bank can refer its customers who want investment services to the ScotiaMcLeod guy. In British Columbia they now say that stock brokers and investment brokers can be trained and hold an insurance licence.
You are going to have this guy with this plaid jacket and hat. He is a broker and also an insurance agent, and he is on the property. You are not supposed to do that under the federal legislation. You cannot advertise your insurance services in the bank, so what are you going to do?
What we have is a spectre in British Columbia of the bank passing on to the investment broker information about the customer who wants investment services, and that broker is also the insurance agent.
This law says that the bank cannot pass on to its insurance subsidiary any personal information about its customers. It can only do direct mailing and advertising via its credit card. Isn't this amazing? We have this guy who is both broker and insurance agent and he is doing all kinds of things, all kinds of synergies around the cages. This is absolutely fantastic. But there it is.
There is another anomaly. If the banks set up an insurance subsidiary, the bank is not allowed under the legislation to pass information about its customers directly to the subsidiary. Yet an insurance company which owns a trust company can pass all sorts of information to its insurance company without any restrictions at all. There is an anomaly in the legislation if what is good for one is not good for the other.
We say there should be harmonization. It seems to us, and we have said this time and time again, that in fact there should be a national task force organized involving the provinces to harmonize the rules that govern financial institutions. In fact, Madam Speaker, I am prepared to go even further. I will stick my neck out and say that if the provincially incorporated financial institutions want access to the federal deposit insurance and to the clearing system, then they ought to conform to federal rules. If they don't, they can set up their own deposit insurance, as Quebec has done, and they can make their own arrangements with respect to clearing. But I expect that would be very difficult for them to do. But you have to have some standard rules by which everybody is playing. You cannot have one playing off against the other.
The next aspect of this bill that bothers us, Madam Speaker, is what is called foreign entities coming into Canada and entering the Canadian financial markets. Of course, we know that on election day 1988 the Minister of Finance of the time announced that American Express would be a bank. That opened up the door. This bill confirms that foreign non-banks can come in any time they want and they can choose how they want to come in. They can come in, of course, as an insurance company or a trust company; they can come in as Sears Financial or Toyota Financial or BCCI. They don't even have to be a bank, they can come in. And it seems to me that if none of these structures fit them-insurance company or whatever-they can always have the option, brother, they can always have the option of going provincial. So you can come in provincially. If what is
September 26, 1991

there federally does not fit you, you can go provincial and do all those things.
I might just say, with respect to the free trade agreement with the United States, that Canada gave away the store on financial institutions and we got no equivalent access to the American market.
Now, that is not just the NDP, Madam Speaker. I want to quote from Linda McQuaig's latest book The Quick and the Dead, page 172, when she says:
Canada also gave considerable ground in the key area of financial services where barriers to entry had traditionally been strongest. Under the Canada-U.S. agreement, for instance, American banks, security firms and insurance companies would be entitled to virtually the same privileges as their Canadian equivalents in the Canadian market.
And Doug Peters, who is the senior vice-president and chief economist at the Toronto Dominion Bank said this: "There is no particular breakthrough in the free trade agreement to allow Canadian banks any greater access to U.S. markets than they already have".
Nothing has changed.
The other area I want to touch on is the area of joint ventures. I have been very concerned about the fact that there are approximately 900 single industry towns across this country. In most of them the banks and major financial institutions have branches and they do very well. They take the deposits of the people of the community. But when the industry on which the town is based goes down the tubes, brother they are out of town, first on the Greyhound heading for Toronto. So where is the social responsibility?
I looked for some flexibility in this bill because I know that the Bank Act, for example, forbids a bank from any kind of commercial involvement in terms of taking equity. I looked for some flexibility within this bill to see if there is a provision whereby under certain very specific and approved conditions, banks can live up to their social responsibility in those single industry towns. I do not think it is fair that it has to be some government agency that gives a grant or backs a loan and takes the chances and the risks all the time. Them that has been getting ought to give sometimes.

In conclusion, our concerns are very clear.
No Sumo wrestlers.

Absolutely no Sumo wrestlers, my friend. Give this man the prize. He was listening. No Sumo wrestling, we want good old fashioned Yukon Erics and Hulk Hogans. We want these institutions to concentrate on serving Canadians, to do the things for which they have received the charter. We want them back in their cages and we want the locks snapped shut on them.
We want to apply the ownership rules to all financial institutions. I recognize that some are very small financial institutions. But one of the witnesses we heard was Canada Trust, which is as large as a bank and would like to become a bank, but in fact cannot.
I believe the 10 per cent rule should be applied to financial institutions. We should strictly enforce non-financial upstream ownership and no downstream financial involvement.
We want a restriction on their entry into the real estate market. That is very dangerous; very dangerous.
Harmonization; it has to come. I saw a reference to it in the constitutional proposal. It has to come. We cannot have this patchwork of rules all across the country and people dipsy-doodling and doing whatever they want to do all over the place. What they cannot do here, they will do there. You cannot have rules in conflict. You cannot increase the cost to financial institutions to comply with all of these rules.
Foreign entries into Canadian financial markets, I say, it is quid pro quo. You do not come in unless you are a bank. If you come in, you obey the Canadian financial institution rules. You have to be a financial institution.
Joint ventures-I appeal to the government to consider putting into the act some provisions with the appropriate safeguards to permit, whatever those safeguards might be. It may be a limited equity for a short period of time in a specific single industry area, but where the banks and financial institutions can live up to some community responsibility, a responsibility to the community in which they have operated.

Government Orders
We intend to go to the committee to try and get these changes. In the last session, on Bill C-83, the last time we dealt with the Trust and Loans Act, which is now Bill C-4, we attempted to make some changes. I sensed there was no support among, particularly, the government members, so I did not put the amendments that I wanted to put. I am saving them for the report stage.
They deal with these questions. I do not see any problem with banks marketing insurance which is developed and owned by insurance companies, because they will get around it anyway and all you are doing is putting a cost up anyway.
It will close small businesses.

The fact is it will not close small businesses. That is a good point, so let us deal with it. How will they close small businesses? The insurance companies will own the insurance policies. The bank is marketing their insurance. In any case, the bank is already setting up its subsidiaries to market the insurance. So if the brokers are concerned, they should be concerned with the banks doing what they are doing now.
Come to Quebec, it is not too bad.

In other jurisdictions, in Europe, those same insurance companies that do not want the banks to market insurance have subsidiary financial institutions that market insurance, and it has not done anything to the marketplace.
In fact, I will tell you what the banks are doing: they are going right into the insurance companies and raiding their brokers. They are taking their brokers, who are already trained, and putting them into their insurance subsidiaries. So they are already doing it.
Madam Speaker, we are going to try in the committee to put a human heart into the bill and a human face on financial institutions. I hope I have explained it well here today so that everybody understands how these beasts operate. Now, Madam Speaker, let us get them back in the cages, put the lock on them, and that is it.

Madam
Speaker, I listened with great attentiveness to the speech of the member for Nickel Belt and there were many points that he raised where I agreed with him completely-
However, there were also many parts of his speech when he talked about the concentration of power with the banking institutions, for instance, he reminded me of Conrad Black. I never thought I would see the day in this House when the member for Nickel Belt would be promoting such a concentration of power in the banking institutions. I really could not quite understand where he was coming from.
What I hear from many small, medium-size and even larger corporations in this country is that there is a concentration of power in the lending institutions and there is a perceived feeling that there is very little competition. In other words, if I am a small or a medium-sized businessman and I go to my comer Royal Bank or Bank of Nova Scotia, and if I am turned down, generally speaking I feel that this is the end of the road for me.
I think that is one of the problems we have in this country right now. The Minister of Finance can stand up here and quote statistics day in, day out, about how interest rates have come down to 9.5 per cent or 9.25 per cent and all the banks post these interest rates with posters and all the rest. Then small business goes in and tries to get a loan and they have no luck because the credit is limited in the country and the reserves of capital have been used up.
My understanding of this bill-and I am coming to my question for the member-is that the insurance companies with large pools of capital will now be able to come into the marketplace and be in a better position to assist those small and medium sized businesses with proper loans.
I would never have thought that the member for Nickel Belt would have seen that as a bad thing, to help small and medium sized business by giving the major banks more competition. I would like to ask him why he sees it like that. We have a regulator and we have a superintendent, so why is he against creating more hope, market or opportunity for the small and medium sized businessman to get at other sources of capital to expand business?
September 26, 1991

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question.
I want to suggest that he look at the plethora of options that a small business person has. I mean, there are credit unions and these credit unions are in every community. Their mandate is to serve the community. I am a member of the credit union where I live and we have a board. Small businesses apply and get loans. We have that.
What I am saying in my speech is that in fact what this bill does is open up the cages, and no insurance company is even close to the size of a bank. The danger is that the banks will eat them up. You will wake up one morning and the dream that you have of insurance companies actually having pools of capital that they want to get into will not be the story they are telling us. That is why they want to demutualize. With all these pools of capital, they want to become banks. But from all the evidence we have heard we are over-banked. They are going to start eating each other up, and that is the danger.
If you really want to protect the marketplace, do not open up the cages and let the lions eat the mongoose and the rabbits and the cobras, but have regulations built in that allow them to do the things that you want them to do.
I do not buy the argument that by allowing insurance companies to become banks this great competitive market will be created.
I mentioned to you in my speech what happened in California. When Ronald Reagan deregulated the whole idea was to allow more players to come in. There would be more money around, more credit and all the rest of it. What is the situation today? There are two major banks in California and soon there may be only one.
We have the same experience with the airline industry. Deregulate the airline industry, take the rules out, and you will encourage more people to put money into the airline business. Today we have two airlines. They are both shaky and there is talk that there will only be one. This bill is about deregulation, brother. I am telling you that if you let the animals out of the cage you will not have any competition in the long run. Sure, in the short run you are going to have a lot of little fish out there lending money, but in the long run they will all be gone like the dodo. That is what I am saying.

Madam Speaker, I

would just like to clarify what my colleague has said dealing with the selling of insurance by financial institutions.
I understand that there were questions raised during this speech as to: "My gosh, would this be in the interest of the consumer? Would this be in the interest of even the insurance brokers?"
I have heard this debate before. In fact I have participated in in this debate in Quebec. Perhaps my colleague from Vancouver would be interested in this debate involving Quebec, because the Caisse Populaire Desjardins wanted to get into the business of selling insurance. We held hearings. They were lengthy hearings dealing with whether the Caisse Populaire Desjardins should sell insurance. Essentially the brokers came by and said: "If you do, we are going to lose our jobs. If you do we will not have a better price for the insurance that is being sold. Finally if you do, you are going to end up controlling the market".
I argued against these points because I said it was nonsense. It has been a very good experience for the past five years. The Caisse Populaire Desjardins has not abused its position. There has not been a single complaint of tied selling. We have been watching it very carefully.
Also, if we say that the bottom line has to be competition, and I agree it has to be, then as the hon. Liberal colleague had said it should bring down prices and make for better service, and it does. Not a single job that I can see has been lost from this increase in competition.
I just want to mention something concerning partisan debate. If we cannot accept that members of the NDP or members of the other parties can say things which other members might feel does not quite fit in ideologically as they see us, if we cannot get beyond that, how far can we go in this debate? In this House reasoned debate should prevail, and I mean reasoned debate, not just partisan debate. That is part of it. As someone coming from Quebec, I know the Quebec situation and have lived through this question of whether banks be allowed to sell insurance. Having had this debate, I would ask you to do your homework or at least come to Quebec.

September 26, 1991
Government Orders
We know what the benefits are for consumers. If the bottom line for Liberals and Conservatives is protection of consumers, then get out of your partisanship and take a look at what happens elsewhere. Come to Quebec and you will see that the reasons that you invoked do not work. No one will lose their job. Prices will be more competitive and consumers will be better served in the long run.
Competition is where it is at. You should be in favour of competition and not just simply the NDP.

Very briefly, Madam Speaker, I just wanted to add that when my colleague, the hon. member Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca, was the premier of British Columbia, they brought in the public auto insurance. Who do you think was given the task of selling it? The credit unions and the agents. The brokers did not lose their jobs. People in rural communities and cities could get their insurance through their credit union or their broker. No one lost their jobs.
I just want to touch, for my good friend in the Liberal Party for whom I have a great deal of respect, on this question of competition. I want to say from the heart that this business of competition is not some altar where we have to go and genuflect and worship. Often when you open up things without proper regulations and controls, it is the strongest who will survive. There is no respect for those who are not able for one reason or another to compete. You need strong referees. You need strong rules. I think that is what we want, fairness in the system.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise and speak on the legislation before the House dealing with financial institutions. It was also very enjoyable to listen to the hon. member for Nickel Belt give his rendition of financial institutions and his feebled fable about caging all of the different institutions. My worry is that if we carry the NDP approach to its logical conclusion, we would have all of our institutions caged. We have all been to zoos and seen exactly what happens with a bunch of caged animals. They have no life, no vitality, no will to really do anything. What we have to do is try to strike the right balance in our system
so that we do have that measure of competitiveness and aggressiveness and those types of things tied in with the proper regulations so that the consumer is protected.
My colleague from Malpeque has given a very extensive discussion on the pieces of legislation before the House. I want to talk in some measure about the Co-Operative Credit Association Act and what is going to happen there. As well, I just want to talk about our financial institutions generally and where they are going with the legislative program before the House.
As background, all agreed that we would come forward with legislation in all four pillars of financial institutions and deal with them all at the same time. We now have all those pieces of legislation before the House.
Quite frankly, it is hoped that we have the will to deal with all of this legislation quickly. I would not want to recount the history of how long it has taken us to get to where we are today, but I believe that most of the financial institutions have been worn down to such an extent that they are fully supportive of the legislation only to move forward and get something done as far as financial institutions are concerned.
In fairness, I think there is a good compromise in much of the legislation that was brought forward. We on this side of the House will be supportive of this legislation going to committee, getting the input that is necessary and giving us an opportunity to make the necessary changes to fine tune the legislation and allow us to come forward with better legislation.
In dealing with the Co-operative Credit Association Act and the legislation in that area, I think we are presented here in Canada with an opportunity to strengthen this organization. It is a good organization. A lot of people are members of credit unions or co-operatives. They know of their involvement in the community. They know the commitment that credit unions and co-operatives have to individual members. It is that approach that is going to help the consumer as we proceed in these very difficult times with globalization, increased competition from outside our borders and with all the problems associated with that particular area.
September 26, 1991

Co-ops can provide that measure of personalized service that is of concern to the individual which larger financial institutions may not provide.
I believe that the co-op movement has made a tremendous contribution to our economy and it is now opening up other opportunities. I think they can make that contribution to the small business person and to the individual because they make a lot of their decisions not on the basis of high-falutin theories and programs that have designations as to who qualifies and who does not. They do it on the basis of the individual. They size up the loan, in large measure, on the basis of the individual. It would be nice to see that at least one financial institution is capable of looking at loans on that basis.
This legislation also provides a benefit to the co-op or the credit union in the sense of allowing them to raise capital. One of the problems credit unions have faced, and indeed all co-ops have faced, is that the only way they can raise capital to do business is either through the sale of memberships or through debt. This legislation is going to give them an opportunity to raise capital through equity. That is a positive step and I compliment the government on that.
I look forward to hearing what the credit unions and co-operatives have to say in that particular area, as to whether the legislation works or whether there should be other ways to assist credit unions in raising capital.
All in all, the legislation is a very thick document that covers a broad range of items. I think it will bring the credit union into a situation in which it is competitive with the other financial institutions and will give it an opportunity to make its contribution to our economy.
If I can, I would like to move from the credit unions and talk generally about financial institutions. The buzzword that we hear all the time is this business of "competitiveness". It is interesting to watch the NDP trying to turn itself inside out and accomplish competitiveness in one sense and be non-competitive in every other sense.
It would be nice if it could get its act together and go down on one side of the issue or the other, rather than around the circle as it has this morning.
My hon. friend says that it does not know what it is doing, and I think this morning was a clear indication
Government Orders
that it has not got the foggiest idea of how the economy runs. Its members have all left. I am sorry, I am not supposed to mention that they have all left. I guess they did, but I am not supposed to say that, so I withdraw that reference to the fact that they are no longer here.
They went right for the gate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The more I listen, the more I think it is the hon. member for Moncton who is running around the rules.

Madam Speaker, I accept your admonition.
I would like to say that there is a tremendous opportunity for us to put our financial institutions into a very competitive mode, to deal with the things that are happening in the global economy and to bring benefit to consumers.
I think we all agree that competition will lower prices to consumers, present new and different products and do all those things that will ultimately be beneficial to consumers. In our attempt to heighten competition we must be very vigilant in order to have those protections in our system so that we may protect consumers as well from those types of calamities that have occurred in the United States, with the failure of the savings and loan organizations and with the number of banks that have gone under.
We in Canada have not escaped unscathed. We have seen what has happened with Standard Trustco and BCCI, the Bank Credit Commerce International. We have to be vigilant and we have to make sure that the supervisory role and regulations are in tact.
As we have heightened competition we must also protect the downside by heightened supervision so that those institutions remain strong and vibrant.
I notice as well in the recent document coming down dealing with our Constitution we have recognized the opportunity that a restructured Canada and a restructured Constitution will be present for financial institutions.
Reading a report in The Globe and Mail of September 25 in the "Report on Business", there is the hope that coming out of some of the constitutional changes there will be the removal of some of the duplication and harmonization of rules and regulations.

Government Orders
I will quote from one of the articles in there which is headlined "A Ray of Hope for the Financial Sector: Ottawa aims to deal with duplication of trust company security regulations". The article goes on to say that the industry has long argued against duplication of financial service regulations and would prefer being governed by one national set of rules as the banks are.
I think that is a positive step, if we could move toward that particular area. That will require the provinces and the Canadian government to work out an acceptable arrangement.
It is mentioned in the document, talking about the streamlining of proposals and avoiding duplications between the different levels of government, and all will benefit as a result of that.
I should say as well that I am concerned about the Canada-Mexico-U.S. trade deal as it relates to financial institutions. We got caught in the last round of negotiations in which we opened our borders and the Americans did not. We did not get the access to the different marketplace items that we were supposed to obtain in the negotiations.
