I am very much concerned that as we proceed into the next phase and deal with Mexico, we will face roughly the same problems because Mexico has a very closed, restricted area of financial institutions. We will be opening up our institutions to the involvement of Mexico's financial institutions and we may not get the quid pro quo of being able to deal in that country and to have the financial institutions of this country in the Mexican economy.
As I have indicated, we in the Liberal Party are supportive of the general direction, the thrust of the legislation. We are looking forward to the opportunity of getting the advice and the contribution from the many institutions and sectors that are affected. We are looking forward to being able to make positive contributions to the debate on our financial institutions. We must do something to strengthen those institutions, to allow them to compete in the global sense, to allow them to provide to our consumers a wide range of products, and at the same time give our consumers the protection to know that their investments in those institutions are safe and that those institutions are sound.
Thank you, Madam Speaker, for the opportunity to address you on this matter.

Madam Speaker, I congratulate my colleague from Moncton. I want to come at this debate from a little different angle today because I think that most of us in this country have a different experience with banks than quite often we talk about in this House.
I have been walking the streets of my riding a lot in the last few months because the House has not been in session. Because we have a severe downturn in the economy a lot of the banking institutions have very tough lines of credit. What I hear quite often from businessmen and home owners is that the banks of this country seem to want to lend you money when you do not need it, but when you really need it they seem to want to shut you down; they do not seem to have any to give you.
A small businessman came to me the other day and said: "They announced the bank rate and the Bank of Montreal the other day reduced its prime rate to 9.5 per cent". The fellow got all excited and he went over to the bank and the bank manager said: "Yes, that is our rate but I do not have any money to lend you".
I hear this more and more and more in this country. I have had experiences myself with banking institutions in this country in which I have found on many occasions, not on every occasion, the bank managers to be very regimented in their thought process. I found them not to be very creative. I have found that their lives seem to be run by the central office, Bay Street. In other words, the head office will send out a memo that they are to cut back on lines of credit, or they are not to lend any more money out, or they are going through an added process whereby "before you advance money double check with us".
This does two things. It takes away from the creativity of the bank manager this centralized control. I am going to repeat myself a lot in the House over the next few weeks until I really feel that we can get to the government on this.
The second thing is that it really works against the hope factor that entrepreneurs need if they are going to grow, take chances and create jobs in this country. Quite often there is a fine line between continuing the fight to stay in business during tough times and just throwing in the towel.
September 26, 1991

I had a very specific situation just a month ago. There were a couple of doctors in my community who rescued a manufacturing firm in Woodstock, Ontario. The name of the firm is Amertek. It makes the finest fire truck in North America, probably the most unique fire truck in the world, so unique that it has received orders from the U.S. military. It has outbid American and European manufacturers. Currently this Amertek fire truck guards the President of the United States at the White House and also at Camp David. This fire truck served in the Persian Gulf and when its competitor fell flat because of the heat and sand conditions the Canadian fire truck was the only one that rose to the occasion. As a result of that it got additional orders.
To get to that point it needed a lot of additional research and development and as a result there was a tremendous strain on its line of credit with the bank. I am not going to mention the bank because I do not want to cause embarrassment to the bank and I do not want to cause any backlash for this great Canadian manufacturing firm, Amertek.
It went through a shocking experience because as it was putting this new order on line, and just as it was getting it rolling, about to deliver its first batch of trucks, the bank manager came back and cut its line of credit by 20 per cent without notice. It had payrolls to meet, suppliers to meet, and it just could not believe it, without notice. I should not say without notice. It naturally had some discussion with the bank manager but obviously after losing in this discussion the bank manager just called up one day and said its line of credit was cut by close to 20 per cent.
Thanks to the Canadian Commercial Corporation which is under the minister of trade this company was rescued. It is delivering its fire trucks. It has another order from Egypt. It has 180 of the finest craftsmen in the country working in Woodstock, and on and on it goes.
I do not believe the centralized power of the banking institutions in this country is right. I do not believe it is serving the Canadian taxpayer. I do not believe it is serving small and medium sized businessmen. I realize that we need to have credit regulations. I support the idea of making sure that the Superintendent of Financial Institutions has access to books and records of all financial institutions, but what I am against is this feeling that there are five or six major banks in this country.
Government Orders
There is a perception that they are a clique and they are all in the same bathtub. If you are shut out at one bank, you are basically shut out at all five.
Somehow we need to communicate to small and medium sized businessmen especially that there are other options. There are other options for capital out there. We can go back to the committee and make adjustments on certain aspects, but the main thrust of this bill I totally support. We need more competition in the financial arena. We need to create more hope in the marketplace for small and medium-sized entrepreneurs in this country.
Just this Monday I talked to the chairman of a major trading house in downtown Toronto. We talked about the fact that there seemed to be so little capital in the market, so little capital for banks to lend to get the economy going again. There have been such large borrowings because of our deficits, not only federally but provincially, which are causing a tremendous strain on our dollar, pushing it upward because of the offshore conversions. However, there are many insurance companies that do have large pools of capital. So, from my reasoning, any effort that would allow a restructuring so that those pools of capital could be more readily available to those smaller and medium-sized businesses is a good thing for the country.
If business has a feeling of confidence in the sense that it is properly financed, then the entrepreneurial spirit naturally is willing to take more risk, and in that process of taking more risk it is going to create more jobs. If we can create more jobs, it is going to put less pressure on our unemployment insurance disbursements, our welfare disbursements and our refugee fund for that matter.
Right now the problem we have in this country is that we have about two million people unemployed. We have entrepreneurship in this country that is almost in a frozen stiff mode. It is basically working from month to month. There is a nervousness and a low morale out there in terms of business. Their bank lines are tight, there is not a lot of cash going around and, as a result, they are not taking any chances.
I know the hon. member from Mississauga supports this. What we have to do is somehow figure out a way to get that entrepreneurial spirit unleashed again. Right now, I believe the best way to do that is try and let that

September 26, 1991
Government Orders
entrepreneurial spirit have a feeling that just because businesses are turned down at one of the major banks in this country, it is not the end of the line.
The member for Mississauga South mentioned to me earlier today that there are about 55 banking institutions in this country to which business has access. That is an important point to know, because I believe that most of us who come from a small business background have a perception there is only the big five banks. Most people do not realize that there is a whole litany of financial institutions out there. I think somehow we, in this House, have to promote the fact that there are a lot of financial institutions.
However, I think that the insurance companies, which have these large pools of capital, should, with regulation, be given the opportunity-and maybe we can do this in committee-to organize their lending practices in a way that it can meet certain social objectives. The member for Chambly says it will not happen. The converse is that if we do absolutely nothing, we keep the status quo. Keep them in their cages. I cannot support that right now and I will tell you why I cannot support it. I have not seen any sign from the major lending institutions in this country that their attitude toward small and medium sized business es going to change without some other competitors coming at them.
The member has a different view than I do and I do respect his experience in Quebec. I would also like to refer to the experience in Quebec of the member for Chambly, and I stand to be corrected, where the caisse de depot et placement will actually go out and invest in smaller and medium-sized business and convert equity in that business into loans. Is that not correct?
I can handle something like that. I wish that our major lending institutions would be more progressive. You have to understand where I am coming from. I am trying to unleash the entrepreneurial spirit that exists in this country.
Right now the mechanisms we have in place are not doing that. I think that the caisse de depot system of investing in small and medium-sized businesses is a great one. I think that that idea should be promoted and
expanded to every region of the country. I think it is a progressive measure.
We need something similar in southern Ontario right now. If we had a situation like this, then an organization like Amertek, which was nearly put out of business a month ago had it not been for the rescue-and it was a constructive approach from the Canadian Commercial Corporation-we would have lost that potential. I am behind this bill. Until I am convinced otherwise, I have to stay my ground.
The other thing my colleague, the member from Prince Edward Island talked about was the commercial complaint section. Very few people who do business with banks realize that there is a commercial complaint section. This is a new feature of the bill, where all of the complaints have to be registered in the Superintendent of Financial Institutions' report. I think that is a very important feature for the people of Canada to understand.
If any one of us as members of Parliament or anyone in business makes a mistake, we certainly are accountable. If we are perceived to have done something wrong, we get up in the morning and read about ourselves on the front page of any paper of this country or see ourselves on national television. It seems to me that the financial institutions of this country have some kind of a special sort of status. They are protected from being challenged when they are not treating consumers fairly. I like that particular aspect of the bill, where there is a consumer complaint section, so that if someone feels that they are not being treated fairly, they have access. They have a recourse. In other words, if you feel the local branch manager is not treating you fairly under this new bill, you now can call the consumer complaint section, put your complaint forward and that actual complaint, whether it is justified or not, has to be reported by the Superintendent of Financial Institutions. I think that is a good thing.
I certainly support the New Democratic Party's view on credit unions. The credit unions in this country, which have done a fantastic job in western Canada especially, do not seem to be as high profile in my part of the country, the Toronto region. I think there is an option of opportunity there in putting forward the services that
September 26, 1991

credit unions have. I am certainly not against credit unions.
All in all, the point that I want to make is that the major banking institutions in this country right now, perceived or otherwise, do not seem to be putting forth an image that they are there to really motivate, to assist the entrepreneurial spirit in this country. I have met many bank managers in my career and some of them are downright smug. Can you believe it?
We have to communicate in a constructive way with our lending institutions the fact that as their attitude towards entrepreneurship in this country goes, so goes our general economy. Anything that will advance the competitive spirit, anything that will advance a greater respect to the spirit that drives this country and creates jobs, I must get behind. Unless in committee this bill can prove to me to do otherwise, I am in total support of it.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. friend one question. He says he supports the bill because he has a real problem with the way banks have operated.
Can he explain to me how come he is in bed with the banks, because the banks want this bill. They want it. I want to know if he cannot see that the banks are the powerful ones now and they will become more powerful with these added provisions.
For example, already one of the banks is in the development business. It is going to build a big building for Ontario Hydro. The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce is already a developer. Can he not see that loosening up and opening the cages will do exactly what he does not want them to do? In fact, he is on the same side as the bankers with respect to this bill. Why does he think they want it?
If they thought it was in any way going to encroach on their power, they would be furiously lobbying every member of this House. Yet he is on the same side as the banks in wanting this bill. I find that rather contradictory.

Madam Speaker, I have enormous respect for the member for Nickel Belt. This is only the beginning of my fourth year in the House of Commons. I watched him for years before that when I had the privilege of working in Mr. Trudeau's office. I have always thought that he made a lot of sense.
Government Orders
I cannot believe I am working against myself on this bill. This bill is going to committee and as I said in speech, if this bill is not going to meet the objectives of creating a more competitive market, if this bill is not going to do some of the things that the caisse de depots in Quebec are doing for smaller and medium-sized business, if this bill is not going to stimulate an attitude which will allow more capital to come into the market, then I have a different view of this bill than you do.
Just because bankers want it does not mean to say that there are not aspects of the bill that cannot serve the general good. I do not see this as consolidating the banking institutions any more. How can it be consolidating the banking institutions position when, in fact, we are creating more competitors for them?
It is not just the insurance companies. It is foreign institutions. I stand to be corrected on that by the member for Mississauga South. Is this not going to allow more foreign institutions-

You can use BCCI as an example. I think AMEX, American Express, is a good example. I was reflecting on that when my colleague for Malpeque spoke earlier.
The American Express approval by the cabinet is something that I do not think we have ever taken full advantage of in this country. We think of American Express right now, most of us in terms of a green card or for a few of us, a gold card. But it dawned on me today while listening to my colleague from Malpeque in this House that the American Express is no different today from the Bank of Montreal or the Bank of Nova Scotia.
Maybe we should be telling that to all our small and medium size businesses, telling them to go out there and test it. This is again where we talk about broadening the competitive base. I am not against American Express having a banking charter as long as it lives up to the responsibilities and duties of a banking institution. If we find from small business and others across this country that it is not lending money, well then I think we bring it back to the committee and say it is a farce, it is a joke. However, we have not tested that yet.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to question my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood because I thought that in his brief intervention he made considerable sense.

Government Orders
What I was having trouble with was the hon. member for Nickel Belt's speech which, while lengthy, left me confused as to the position of the New Democratic Party. I know that the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood is not an expert on that, but he heard the speech of the hon. member for Nickel Belt and I wonder if he could illumine us. What is the position of New Democratic Party members? They say they favour increased competition, at least with insurance companies. I thought they said they were in favour of allowing banks to take over insurance companies and offer insurance as part of a package.
Oh, no.

I heard the hon. member for Chambly say that he supported the fact that Quebec caisses were able to sell insurance as well. He said if it was good for them to be able to sell it, it must be all right for banks to sell it. Yet now they are saying that is not their position, that it is not okay for banks to sell it. Or, is it? I think the hon. member for Nickel Belt is terribly confused. I wonder if the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood was able to make more sense out of that speech than I was.

Madam Speaker, my colleague from Kingston and the Islands is making this very difficult for me. I was, as I said in my previous question, a bit confused by the member for Nickel Belt. I can tell you that subsequent to his speaking I walked along the hall and spoke to him because I did not understand where he was coming from. To my colleague for Kingston and the Islands, in fairness he did-not in the House but behind the curtain-clarify some of his points of view. If I could dare-
To put words in his mouth.

To put words in his mouth, right. The member for Nickel Belt is not against competition. He is not against helping small and medium sized business. We have a different point of view. He is concerned about the fact that it is only going to be short-term competition by allowing these other financial institutions to compete in the free flow of capital.
I differ from that view. I think it will be more than a short-term gain. I think it will produce a long-term benefit to everyone. With respect to his point about being concerned about people losing their jobs, I would need more information on that because I cannot see that.
As far as the member for Chambly goes, I like his idea about the caisse de depot et de placement investing in small and medium size businesses. I wish we could figure out a way to steal that idea from Quebec and bring it to Ontario and other parts of the country. I wish our larger financial institutions would maybe take a page out of the caisse de depot's book.

Madam Speaker, I enter the debate only for the purpose of going over in this House some of the history of this legislation and the great deal of work that has been done by members on all sides of the House in actually formulating the bills we have before us and Bill C-4 that has been dealt with by the finance committee.
First of all, this issue became an important issue in 1982. The then government formed a committee called the Dimma committee. It studied the re-regulation of banks and other financial institutions, trust companies, insurance companies and the like.
After the 1984 election, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, then Minister of State for Finance, produced a green paper. That green paper was an analysis of the financial companies that we had in the country. Immediately after that paper, the finance committee of this House made a thorough study of the financial implications of the green paper and produced for the House a very long report.
That long report was to some extent influenced by the collapse of the Canadian Commercial Bank, the Northland Bank, and the collapse in that one year alone of one trust company, mortgage company or insurance company every month in 1985.
We have done a great deal of work here. As a result of the report of the finance committee and as a result of the report of the Estey Commission inquiring into CCB and Northland as a result of the work by the Senate, the government produced a blue paper under the auspices of the hon. member for London West who was then Minister of State for Finance.
That paper met a great deal of discussion right across Canada, with every institution and members on all sides of this House. I particularly remember the efforts of the member for Kamloops who was leading for the New Democratic Party on the finance committee at that point. He was followed up by the hon. member for
September 26, 1991

Ottawa Centre, Michael Cassidy, a former member. Raymond Garneau and Mrs. Nicholson from Toronto of the Liberal Party both worked very diligently with the committee trying to work out how these institutions might be organized and how the legislation might be worked out.
I want to say that the legislation that we have is non-partisan legislation developed as a result of a great deal of consultation and work by members of this House going back to the Parliament of 1981, 1982 and 1983 and moving forward since then.
This legislation has the approval of almost every person involved in the insurance industry in this country, almost every person involved in the credit union movement in this country, almost every person involved in the trust company industries in this company, and the approval of the Canadian Bankers' Association across the board.
They all have their own little extra that they would like out of the bills. We are going to have to make some arbitrage there, but the leading spokesman of every one of these organizations and their lobby groups has been to see me as the former chairman of the finance committee and other members of this House. They have said how important this legislation is in order to re-regulate and make things work in a more modern way for the good of us all.
While we have done a lot of work, we have more work to do in the finance committee in terms of making sure that the bills work as well as they can. I think this House should be commended for the effort particularly of members of the House for making sure that the bills are the kind of bills they are and are now before the House.
This is a non-partisan bill. This is not an NDP bill, a Liberal bill or a Conservative bill. This bill has been developed by this Parliament, the previous Parliament and the previous Parliament by members deliberately working together to come to grips with the issue.
I think we have some more work to do, but we ought to move ahead as quickly as we can to make sure the matter receives that detailed consideration that it must yet receive.

Madam Speaker, I was listening very carefully to what the hon. member was saying. I also particularly respect what he has to say
Government Orders
because of his experience on the finance committee as chairman.
He mentioned in passing-and I find it very intriguing-that he feels that there is some work to do. That means that he is not completely satisfied with the bill. I am sure that there is no bill which is perfect and there is always some work to be done.
I would like him to take this opportunity in a non-partisan way because he is right, it is not an NDP bill. It is far from an NDP bill, I can assure him of that, but it is not a Conservative bill and it is not a Liberal bill. If he has some reservations as he seems to have indicated, I would like to know what they are because perhaps we will find a certain commonality of objections. Perhaps that would also help the committee when it looks further into this question.

Madam Speaker, as I explained to the member for Malpeque, these three bills that we have right here represent a little over three and one-quarter or three and one-half inches of compressed printing. The other bill we have already passed is another inch and a bit of compressed printing. We have a good four and one-half inches or more of compressed printing in trying to develop a financial system.
I think that there are some small conflicts. For example, I see no reason why banks should be required to have two auditors, whereas trust companies and insurance companies can get along with one. I have spoken to people in all of the industries on that. There has been some concern and there is room for some discussion. It just seems to me that it is really the depositor who pays. It is really the insurance person who pays and, if you increase the overhead of an organization, they can pay less in interest to their depositors and they are less efficient.
There have been some representations in connection with insurance companies and their right to borrow in the marketplace. I want to look at that and I want to look at their ability to take in what amounts to deposits.
I think there is some misapprehension around when you talk about insurance staying in insurance and banking staying in banking. None of these institutions have been operating that way for a very long period of time. For example, insurance companies in this country really only do 20 per cent of their business as insurance. That may seem strange but in effect our major life insurance companies are really in the business of selling annuities.

September 26, 1991
Government Orders
They are in the business of selling deposit receipts and in effect they are operating as come to your home bankers.
This legislation brings that into line and so it is important that it be passed. It is important that we understand that the overlaps that already exist in the financial community are very significant. It is important that the regulation of that be as set out pretty well in the bills.
I want to say that at this point what we are really looking at is fine tuning legislation that has had a pretty good run over with the finance committee already. You may recall the hearings held well before Christmas of last year for all the witnesses dealing with a white paper produced by the present minister. It resulted in a great deal of agreement. We then spent a great deal of time on clause by clause consideration of what is now Bill C-4.1 expect that when you are talking about differences and things that must be changed, we are really talking about very minor matters.
To a large extent all of the issues have been in a sense brokered to make sure that it works out that each head of financial responsibility, each pillar if you want to put it that way, has its defined area. That defined area can be easily examined and inspected to make sure of the sanctity of depositors' money, the sanctity of the rights of people who pay premiums for insurance and so on.
We have to make sure that these companies that are given privileges and benefits and are allowed to do a certain class of business in Canada that is really for the benefit of the public, operate for the benefit of the public and operate in a way to ensure the protection of deposits. Our whole work has to be to make sure that these companies operate as well as they can.
I think we are getting there, so when you ask me what has to be done there are only a few things.
Mr. Speaker, I was assuming that at this point we were resuming debate. May I have clarification from the Chair?
Are there any more questions?
No.
Resuming debate. The hon. member for Chambly.

Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to my colleagues and particularly to the former chairman of the finance committee. I found him to be both to the point and concise, and I am going to try to follow his example and do the same thing.
I would like to mention that we must not play any semantic games here. This is a major piece of legislation. This is a piece of legislation that I believe will have major effects on consumers across this country. It is something that has taken three, four, five years to get to this point. It will certainly not harm these institutions which have had record years if we take the time to look seriously at the potential consequences. I feel that in doing so we will benefit consumers generally.
My general feeling here is that if something is not broken why fix it. I am not quite sure that the system as it is now needs the intervention of Parliament, needs this legislation at this time. I must say most emphatically that the NDP is not against competition. We want to see competition. After saying that, we are quite properly against this bill because, after rational analysis, non-partisan I believe because we have looked at the bill itself and not just the ideology, we do not think that this bill provides what it pretends to provide. That is why we have debate going on today.
I would like to mention certain aspects of Bill C-19 and in my comments I would like to target the question of abusive power, possibly, as well as the banks selling insurance.
On banks selling insurance, in one sense we are much in favour of that. As I said I used the Quebec analogy. As a Quebecer I am very pleased to see that Quebec has taken the lead in this. I must respond to what some of my Liberal colleagues have said: "That means that banks should be able to own insurance companies".
September 26, 1991

I am saying that it does not mean that. Quebec has a caisse populaire system, which I am completely in favour with, selling insurance policies.
[ Translation ]
And I would like to explain for the benefit of my Liberal colleagues that a number of years ago, we in Quebec realized that letting credit unions sell insurance could be beneficial to the entire community. I remember we had the same kind of debate in the National Assembly. At the time insurance brokers told us that if we let credit unions sell insurance, they would all lose their jobs.
There were also consumer groups-and this was one of the few times I disagreed with them-who said: If we let credit unions sell insurance, it will cost us a lot more, because they will force us to buy insurance from them by engaging in tied-in selling, which means they won't give us a mortgage or anything else unless we buy insurance from them. They will take advantage of the power they have over the market.
Another objection was that the Caisses populates Desjardins were so powerful in Quebec that they would control the market. I heard my Liberal colleagues saying it can't be done and that jobs will be lost. There were the same old arguments that people would lose their jobs, that it would be a closed market, that there would be so many problems that it would restrict entrepreneurship. All I can say is that in Quebec, speaking of entrepreneurship, I don't think there has ever been any legislation that would be able to reduce the spirit of entrepreneurship in that province.
However, there is a difference when we are talking about letting banks sell insurance on the same terms as the credit unions. Credit unions, and especially the Caisses populaires Desjardins, do not have the same mandate as the banks. A credit union's responsibilities are different, because it is owned by its members. The Caisse populaire Desjardins and other credit unions are not banks. In other words, they are not bankers. My colleague referred to a smug, anti-consumer attitude. Credit unions don't have that attitude, not at all. They are truly integrated organizations, which is to say they are an integral part of the community and reflect the community's needs.
Government Orders
I think it is somewhat exaggerated to say that since the Caisses populaires Desjardins and other credit unions in Quebec sell or market insurance, this means that companies, and especially banks, should have the right to purchase insurance companies. I say no. As was said by the chairman of the Finance Committee-in fact, he was quoted by my colleague from Nickel Belt-let the banks do the banks' work and let other companies do theirs. I think that is very sensible, and I fully endorse my colleague where he quotes the former chairman of the Finance Committee.
I would like to say a few words about abusive powers, because I have worked for a long time as a consumer advocate. I have seem examples of abuse of power by banks. I remember clearly my experience with the Banque nationale du Canada, the BNC. I believe the president at the time was Michel Belanger, one of the joint chairs of the Belanger-Campeau Commission. In my brief to the commission, I mentioned the fact that the Banque nationale du Canada had a certain view of Quebec society, and that it was a corporate view. I do not endorse that kind of view nor the vision of the Banque nationale du Canada as expressed in its actions.
The case I quoted was mentioned in a judgment by the Supreme Court, and I am referring to Houle vs Banque nationale du Canada. The Supreme Court judgment contains a number of facts relating to abusive power, and they are absolutely terrifying. We have a bank that pushed the president or owner of a small business into bankruptcy because it did not give the owner of this small business a chance to pay its debts. It proceeded with a seizure before the judgment, and the gentleman was obliged to declare bankruptcy. !ALP/jcl300-2

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member for Chambly, for the time being, and I am sure he will wish to continue his speech later this afternoon.
It being one o'clock, I do now leave the Chair until 2 p.m.
At 1 p.m. the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.
September 26, 1991

Mr. Speaker, over the last 30 years, Quebec has acquired economic and political institutions to meet its needs. It did so in its own way, with its own resources. The general public and business people are proud of these achievements. Moreover, they are working very hard to make them more effective.
Today the federal government wants to meddle in our affairs. It wants to create new powers, new standards, new agreements and impose them on Quebecers. That is totally unacceptable. First, it will lead to new confrontations and aggravate the existing tensions. Second, it will make the political and legislative process more cumbersome, slow it down and hurt Quebec's economic development.
I therefore call on Quebecers to reject the federal government's constitutional proposal.

Mr. Speaker, the people of El Salvador has endured the devastation, destruction and death of a 12-year old civil war.
Yesterday, leaders of the FMLN and the Salvadoran government signed a peace agreement under the auspices of the UN that brings hope for a ceasefire before the end of the year.
As well, measures agreed to in this peace accord will set a constructive course towards the democratization of the political process in El Salvador.
New Democrats have long supported a peaceful resolution of the civil war and we have consistently raised in the House of Commons concerns of the Salvadoran people regarding human rights violations, international aid and Canada's policies in Central America.
We applaud the efforts of Secretary General Perez de Cuellar for his role in the negotiations that led to this accord and urge both the FMLN and the representatives
of the Salvadoran government to stay the course of peace.

Mr. Speaker, the PVY-N situation in the Canadian Prince Edward Island potato industry has become farcical. The industry has been thrown into chaos. Borders are closed and millions of dollars are lost and now we find that testing proceedings which led to all this are found to be flawed.
In a follow-up test, 8 out of 10 samples originally labelled positive have been found to be negative, an 80 per cent error rate. Agriculture Canada, badly understaffed in the technical area, made a call. That call was in large part wrong.
Now we have a case in Saskatchewan where a tuber imported from the United States has tested positive. This diagnosis was confirmed in three separate labs.
I ask the Minister of Agriculture to intervene in the situation and order a complete retesting program to eliminate the errors made, take action to have the U.S.A. institute a testing program the same as the one forced on P.E.I., apply the same import restrictions against the United States as they have applied against us and, finally, call a full-scale into the entire problem so that once and for all the air will be cleared and the industry will know where it stands, both nationally and internationally.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, aggressive advertising, exchange rates and tax on gasoline are all major factors in the cross-border shopping issue.
Over recent years all members will know that crossborder shopping has been on the rise and same day trips to the U.S. are increasing at an alarming rate in border communities like mine of Sarnia-Lambton.
This trend cannot continue. Cross-border shopping has severe economic consequences for Canada, as well as serious implications for federal and provincial governments. Both are concerned about the negative impact on employment.
September 26, 1991

Both are also losing considerable tax revenues. A study by the consulting firm Ernst and Young estimated the total tax loss, excluding income taxes, was $15 million for 1990 in Sault Ste. Marie alone. So what does this figure mean again? It means tax loss for the provinces and, of course, the retailers are suffering, especially in border communities like mine that is on the leading edge of this phenomenon.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday in Yugoslavia, federal forces in the Republic of Croatia attacked targets in the town of Vinkovci with napalm and cluster bombs.
According to western news sources, one of their targets was a bam that had been converted into a field hospital and was clearly marked with a red cross. Mr. Speaker, as a signatory to the Geneva Convention and the UN Charter of Rights, Canada must denounce the use of napalm and cluster bombs on civilian and Red Cross targets. We must use our influence in the world community to put an end to the atrocities being committed in Croatia.
This is a situation which poses a serious threat to world order. The world stood up and took notice when Saddam Hussein threatened the use of chemical weapons against the innocent people of Kuwait. It must do the same today for the inhabitants of Croatia, and Canada must lead the way.

Mr. Speaker, I sat on the Belanger-Campeau Commission for a long time. I kept quiet out of respect for my colleagues and the institution I represent.
Throughout this commission, people called for a plan for society. They kept asking for economic union. They demanded recognition of the distinct society. I can say that the document the Prime Minister has just presented gives Quebec all that.
The party poopers, bogeymen, eternal skeptics, wreckers, the Bouchards, Laroses, Brassards and their ilk are at work demolishing our house, which is part of our national heritage. The laws covering heritage, in Quebec as in Canada, will not allow these dream merchants, these charlatans to achieve their personal ends by demolishing what Quebecers cherish most: our feeling of belonging and our pride.
And to those who would not know that, I say it in French, in our Parliament in Ottawa.

Mr. Speaker, last week Canada's first female Minister of Justice compromised every feminist principle she claims to espouse. Recently her colleague, the Conservative member of Parliament from Burlington, referred to a female member of the Liberal caucus as a slut.
The Minister of Justice said this was okay because he was provoked. She said the hon. member-

We have a longstanding tradition that in statements by members there should not be a personal attack against any other member in the House. The hon. member is, I think, very much on that course and it does disturb me. If the hon. member wants to finish his statement and make a point, I will of course hear him.

The point is that it is inconceivable that such a dangerously partisan defence of the indefensible would come from the Minister of Justice, who convened a Women and the Law conference and who frequently refers to herself as a feminist.
May I suggest to the minister that she re-evaluate her own principles when she suggests that sometimes a woman deserves to be attacked with such venom and hatred because of her-

Just a moment. The hon. member is a long time and distinguished member of this House and I know that he feels very strongly on the issue. However, I think we ought to proceed and hear another member.
The hon. member for Portage-Interlake.

September 26, 1991

Mr. Speaker, when I asked Deborah Wehrle, a charming law student at the Ottawa Law Society, her opinion on the constitutional package, here is what she said:
The constitutional package presented to Canadians on Tliesday, September 24, sets out an innovative plan to remove barriers to interprovincial trade in Canada. This change will help ensure economic recovery and future prosperity. Let us take a cue from Europe. Diverse European countries have committed themselves to the elimination of trade barriers in a common market to enhance their competitiveness. This sets a fine example. In Canada we are already united as one nation. We have a great tradition of hard work and co-operation. It is time for Canadians to recognize the key to our 124 years old success story. Our country has prospered because of a commitment to rise above our differences, to overcome geographical distances, and pool our strengths.
The Conservative Party is committed to creating a strong domestic market which can compete globally. It is time to focus on creating an effective, internal market and strong economic union to ensure prosperity in Canada in the 21st century and beyond.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk about Algoma Steel.
In May of this year, I asked the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology what he thought of employee ownership. He endorsed the principle. He suggested I speak to the Minister of Finance about it. I asked him in the House of Commons, and he endorsed the principle.
I met with the minister last week. He said: "I cannot give you an answer. I am waiting for the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology", so it is back in his ball court.
If I may, I will quote the Minister of Industry and Science. He said: "I will help Algoma when I am convinced it will dramatically be restructured".
It has been restructured. It is in the process of being restructured. We will lose 1,600 or 1,800 jobs. What is the definition of restructuring to the minister, 3,000 people or when the whole plant is closed down?
We ask the minister to make a recommendation to the Minister of Finance to assist us now, be it tax credits, older worker adjustment, bridge pensions or whatever. We ask them not to be passive spectators at the table for Algoma restructuring. The federal government must participate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Science
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I applaud the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada to send Joseph Kindler and Charles Ng back to the United States.
No longer will Canada be considered by the likes of Ng and Kindler as a safe haven to escape capital punishment.
No longer will the likes of these men consider sliding down the wall on bed sheets to escape justice in the United States.
No longer will the victims in the United States be denied justice in seeing Ng face the charges for the 19 violent murders he is accused of in California.
My thanks go out to all members of this House, the justice committee and victims of Violence International for assisting in this seven year fight to extradite Ng and Kindler. I am doubly pleased to be able to advise the United States victims in the Ng case that they will finally see justice.
In closing, a special thanks to the 185,000 Canadians and Americans who wrote to members of this House of Commons urging for justice to be seen to be done in the United States and to return Ng to the proper justice he deserves.

Mr. Speaker, last Saturday Armenians voted 99.3 per cent in favour of independence, marking the end of 71 years of communist rule.
This was an historic moment for a people so touched by persecution, occupation and natural disaster.
September 26, 1991

In 1915, the genocide at the hands of the Ottoman Empire killed 1.5 million Armenians. Armenia gained independence in 1918, only to be occupied in 1920 by the Soviet Union.
Over the last three years, Armenians have suffered the worst ethnic violence in the republics, with 2,000 killed.
The people of Armenia and the Armenian community here in Canada have dreamed of the day when their country would be independent. Today, we share in that joy.
Armenia faces a number of economic challenges: the exodus of Armenians from Azerbaijan and the 1988 earthquake that left 500,000 homeless.
We look forward to the day when Armenians of Nagorno-Karabakh become part of Armenia. We seek recognition by the world community and Canada of the genocide.
We call upon the Government of Canada to recognize Armenia and to help Armenia achieve its aspirations of becoming a prosperous, democratic nation.

Mr. Speaker, Quebecers are starting to discover the real motives behind the negative attitude of the Bloc Quebecois leader. Every time he opens his mouth, we realize that he has nothing more to propose and that he is only seeking to destroy Canada. His national sport is rejecting out of hand any proposal that does not come from his small mind.
From listening to him, Mr. Speaker, the children and uninformed people in Quebec would end up believing that all the Caisses populates would move to Alberta. Nothing less than a scare campaign from the Bloc Quebecois.
Mr. Speaker, Quebecers will not accept for much longer the permanent indignation and half-truths that come out of the mouths of Bloc Quebecois members. Instead of making concrete proposals, the leader of the
Bloc Quebecois prefers to act in the federal Parliament like a puppet of Jacques Parizeau or Gerald Larose. What a shame for Quebecers!

Mr. Speaker, more than five years ago this government had promised to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Canadians still await this important legislation. Yesterday, Judge Joseph McDonald ruled that the Canadian Human Rights Act is unconstitutional because it fails to protect lesbians, gay men and bisexuals from discrimination. The right to be free from discrimination based on sexual orientation has been put into law in Quebec, the Yukon, Manitoba and Ontario.
I call on this government and this Minister of Justice to introduce long-awaited amendments to the Canadian Human Rights Act. It is time to ensure that Canadian lesbians, gay men and bisexuals can live in dignity and freedom from discrimination.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday was a very important day for anyone concerned with this nation's forests. Our minister announced in Toronto the new program Partners in Sustainable Development of Forests. This initiative will help establish a network of forests that will become working models for sustainable forest development. The model forest will demonstrate the most advanced scientific methods, techniques and forestry practices.
The partners program will promote a broad balance between all users of our forests and demonstrate Canada's commitment to our international responsibilities as one of the world's major forested nations. Through the key partnerships with provinces, with industry, with forest owners, with native groups and environmental organizations, this program is another example of Canada's support for the principle of sustainable development.
Oral Questions THE CONSTITUTION

September 26, 1991

Mr. Speaker, our government recently released a package of proposals to renew the Canadian federation. It is my hope that Canadians will look at these proposals and put forward their concerns and ideas in an open and rational manner. This should not be regarded as an emotional issue. This is primarily about federalism, economics and history.
Canadians are on the brink of undoing that which the European Economic Community has striven toward for 50 years. Quebec separation means the isolation of the maritimes. That could lead to a separate Ontario and a separate British Columbia and hence, the destruction of a country that has developed to become one of the two most preferred countries to live in in the world.
Our country's future is in our hands. Canadians, I urge you to grow up, wake up, familiarize yourselves with our history in order that we may have a future.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance. The Bank of Canada Act says that the Bank's role is to use monetary policy to mitigate "fluctuations in the general level of production, trade, prices and employment-".
The proposals on economic union tabled this morning want to eliminate any reference to production, trade and employment. I therefore ask the Minister of Finance why he wants to take from the Governor of the Bank of Canada the obligation in setting monetary policy to ensure job creation for the unemployed in this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. Leader of the Opposition would share the view that in order to achieve sustainable growth, one must have price stability. There is clearly historical evidence of that fact.
As a matter of fact, if one were to look at some of the leading industrialized nations of the world, particularly looking at Japan and Germany, one would find that they have had excellent growth and more than reasonable price stability.
What this attempts to do is clarify the mandate of the Bank of Canada. It has been criticized in some quarters as being overly broad, ambiguous and can tend to be contradictory on occasion. It is in that respect that we are attempting to clarify the role of the Bank of Canada to achieve price stability, and to achieve price stability, you can achieve sustainable growth with job activity.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government and the Governor of the Bank of Canada have been obsessed with fighting inflation for five years now. Today we have a high for the last six years in unemployment, and we still have a very high level of inflation.
I want to know from the minister why he wants to take away the responsibility of the governor of the bank, in setting the monetary policy, the obligation to look at the unemployed. Why does he want to give a green light to the governor of the bank to not care at all about the level of employment in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there may be a fundamental difference in the goals and objectives of this government as compared to the position of the Liberal Party.
What the leader of the Liberal Party would advocate is high inflation, high interest rates, high deficits, slow growth and high unemployment. That is the record of the past. If one looks at the period in Canada from 1950 to 1973, one will note that there were inflation rates that averaged about 2.8 per cent with growth in excess of 5 per cent. When inflation was up around 9 per cent, the rate of growth fell to about 3 per cent or 3.1 per cent.
It is not only Canada that is pursuing this goal and objective. The over-all goal and objectives of the Group of Seven countries is designed to achieve price stability and sustainable growth. The goals and objectives of the OECD are likewise. Just recently, Mr. Laidler of the C.D. Howe Institute said that the target of price level
September 26, 1991

stability is both appropriate and feasible and the bank's mandate should be updated accordingly.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you can have growth and you can have price stability but you have to make sure in the process that you do not create unemployment in the country. One good way to achieve this is to have an economic union. I am very pleased to realise that at last the government has read the document Securing the Canadian Economic Union in the Constitution that I tabled in this House 10 years ago, and that was opposed by all the members of that party. Never in this document did we want to take away the responsibility from the governor of the bank to look after the unemployed in Canada.
Will this government change its policy and make sure that the monetary policy of Canada takes into account that we have to create jobs for Canadians and zero inflation will not do any good if we have 25 per cent of the population not working? What we want is jobs for Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the best way to create jobs is through sustainable growth and sustainable growth can be achieved through price stability.
I am veiy pleased that the hon. member is pleased about the over-all package. I am sure that he would be pleased to note that in connection with the question that he just put, the document at page 39, in consideration of price stability, says: "Monetary policy should be conducted with due cognizance of the path to price stability that best contributes to other Canadian objectives". One of those Canadian objectives is obviously growth, job creation and economic activity throughout the country from coast to coast to coast.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance.
The minister speaks about doing nothing more than clarifying the mandate of the Bank of Canada, but in the document he tabled today he says "their references to mitigating fluctuations in production trade and unemployment-should be eliminated." That is not elimination, that is massacring.
Oral Questions
If the Minister of Finance is serious about encouraging jobs, production and growth, why does he want to take any references about them out of the mandate of the Bank of Canada? How can he be taken seriously if those words are eliminated?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is being taken seriously because this issue is being taken seriously around the world. Whether it is the Group of Seven industrialized nations, whether it is the OECD group of nations, whether it is the United States, whether it is Japan, whether it is Germany, all are committed to the goals of price stability because if you have price stability you will have sustainable growth and if you have sustainable growth, you will have job creation activity.
Right here in Canada the C.D. Howe Institute which certainly is not a Conservative think tank-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: The hon. member quotes it quite often. I remind the hon. member that the recommendation that was published in a paper by Mr. Laidler said "the target of price level stability is both appropriate and feasible and the bank's mandate should be updated accordingly", and that is precisely what we are doing.

Mr. Speaker, the minister boasts about his policies of price stability. What have they brought us? A made-in-Canada recession, one and a half million people unemployed, our export industries in absolute crisis.
I ask the minister why, through the policies announced today, does he want to continue to enforce forever on Canadians policies of recession and unemployment and force the provinces to do the same thing. Can he explain that to Canadians who are already suffering the burdens of his misguided policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is absurd in his interpretation. I have tried to make that clarification in response to earlier questions. What the hon. member is really proposing is a policy of high inflation, high interest, high deficits, slow growth and high unemployment. Canadians have had enough of that. The only way to achieve sustainable growth is through the containment of inflation and price stability.

September 26, 1991
Oral Questions
All we have to do is look at what has happened in Japan: low inflation, high growth, prosperity. Germany: low inflation, high growth, job creation.
You can go around the country and prosperity is linked very clearly with sustainable growth and price stability, and that is what we are attempting to achieve.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs. Price stability is indeed important but those people who do not have jobs, who cannot buy anything, are more concerned with getting a job and contributing their skills to society.
Yesterday the minister indicated in committee that he might be willing to reconsider the proposal to make reducing inflation the central priority of the Bank of Canada. I ask the minister if he will commit today, and convince his colleague the Minister of Finance, that this party's policy of full employment, is an important priority for the Bank of Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada and Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if my memory is correct, what I said yesterday more precisely was that if the language in our document did not adequately reflect our intention then I would look at a chance to try to make the language more precise.
There is no question at all as my colleague, the Minister of Finance, has said about the commitment of this government to job creation. This is almost a red herring that members of the House are trying to bring across the trail of the House today. That, of course, is their privilege.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the minister. It is essential that jobless men and women find a job, and the unemployment rate causes great concern across Canada. There are 1.5 million unemployed Canadians today. So, I ask the minister again: is he willing now to recognize that full employment should be one of the primary objectives of this government and that the Bank of Canada should do its share too?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada and Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to do two things today. First, I will indicate that the government of Canada fully supports policies based on substantial and permanent employment opportunities across Canada. And it is policies such as the one my colleague the Minister of Finance has just described that can have that effect. Second, if the hon. member has an amendment, an improvement or anything else to propose, she is welcome to do so.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance and the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs talk about the importance of price stability. We are trying to say, simply, open up the process, recognize the reality of Canada, that there are many people out there crying for this government to make sure that they can earn a respectable living. There are many others who need shelter in this country.
I ask the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs this: In the government's proposal it indicates that housing can be made an exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. Many Canadians depend on the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to finance social housing, so I want to ask the minister if his government is to go ahead with the idea of transferring its responsibilities to make sure that the funding that is presently spent for social housing will also be transferred to the provinces.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada and Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of our proposal is to indicate that not simply are we interested in changes in theory in the way federalism operates, we are also prepared to look at specific changes in the way powers are exercised. We are following certain principles here.
One of those principles that we want to follow is a greater respect for the constitutional jurisdiction that has been established. Another is one of efficiency, of trying to have policies carried out by the level of government that is most effective and most able to carry them out.
As I indicated yesterday, in other fields like the environment it is the determination of this government to continue to guard and to keep and to exercise all of the powers that are ours. But we have made it clear that we are prepared to discuss with the provinces means by which there can be a recognition of their exclusive jurisdiction in domains, in fields like housing.
September 26, 1991

I think that as the hon. member considers these proposals she will see that that is a constructive way to give reality to the principles that I think we all in this House espouse of trying to have a more effective federal system, including one that allows provinces like the province of Quebec to take account of the particular challenges and situation that they face.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister.
In the debate on the economic union, we note a great discrepancy between the point of a new hold by Quebec which sees the role of the state as the driving force of economic development and that of the government as expressed in its plan which overlooks it.
So, here is my question: to close yesterday's debate, is the government prepared to entrench in the Constitution the right of the provinces not only to create, but to maintain and innovate on their own initiative, new economic development institutions such as the Quebec Deposit Fund or the Heritage Fund?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps any confusion that may exist over what is in or what is not in the document can be dispelled today with the release of the document. There has been a lot of debate about what the document might contain or what its implications are. With regard to many of the concerns that have been expressed, for example in Quebec about the fact that the federal government would immerse itself into provincial budget-making, I don't think there is anything in the document that reflects that at all.
I think the release of the document will clarify many of the items that the hon. member has referred to.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps something was lost in the translation. I asked, very clearly, if the government was prepared to guarantee within the Constitution the right of the provinces to develop their own economic institutions like the Heritage Fund and the Caisse de depot.
My question now is to the Minister of Industry and Trade. It is not enough to build an economic union that is done on the basis of yesterday's economy, and that is the linkage this government has failed to make. There is not
Oral Questions
much use advocating the free circulation of goods if there are no goods to circulate or nobody to buy them. Will the government undertake specifically in its forthcoming paper on competitiveness to target at least 25 per cent of our Gross National Product as a firm objective for manufacturing in order to give Canadians jobs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member loses his credibility when he makes the statement he just made, that we have not made the linkage between unity and the strength of our economy. That is absolutely clear in the Speech from the Throne and it was absolutely clear in the Prime Minister's statement on Tuesday. It is absolutely clear in the document.
As the member also pointed out, we have these two documents coming out on competitiveness and learning which reinforce the statements we have already made. Clearly, we are going to be putting in place a consultation process that will respond to the questions the hon. member has been asking. In that way we will ensure that we have an increasing degree of export activity, of international activity which will affect the manufacturing sector the hon. member is concerned about.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the President of the Treasury Board why the government has decided, while refusing to budge on the zero per cent increase of salaries to public servants, to continue to give performance pay to over 4,000 managers in the Public Service, in some cases up to 10 per cent of their salaries. Pourquoi ce double standard?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
For the managers of the Public Service, a former government, and I think it was a Liberal government, decided that they would be dealt with in two ways. They took away 15 per cent of the wage budget and decided to have a basic pay. Instead of having, as there is for the unionized employees, the seniority which will go up even if we have the zero per cent unionized, the same treatment is given to the managers.

September 26, 1991
Oral Questions
This is a system that was put in place for the managers who will get zero pay increase and will get the seniority the same as the unionized employees.

Mr. Speaker, let us get this straight. The minister has already said to the press that there would be no increase in bonuses because that is rolled into and considered a part of the salary that would be frozen.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to pay tribute to Senator Stan Waters who passed away yesterday in Calgary after a battle with cancer.
Senator Stan Waters was bom in Winnipeg on June 14, 1920 of English immigrant parents. He was educated in prairie schools including Gameau-Strathcona High School in Edmonton.
In 1933 his parents sent him to England for one year to broaden his educational experience. He then entered the University of Alberta in 1938 before joining the war.
In 1941 Senator Waters left the University of Alberta to join B Squadron of the King's Own Regiment at Stettler as a private, and later that year as a corporal went overseas with his regiment.
On being commissioned in 1942, he volunteered for the newly formed Canadian parachute corps and after training was assigned to the U.S.-Canadian First Special Service Force which specialized in commando and parachute operations.
With the First Special Service Force, Stan fought through the costly mountain battles in southern Italy and the assault landing at Anzio. His unit was the first to enter Rome on June 4, 1944. Stan attained the rank of major when the unit was disbanded. He then joined the First Canadian Parachute Battalion and fought in northwest Europe in 1945.

Tribute
After the war he served in a wide range of command and staff appointments, including command of the Princess Patriot's Canadian Light Infantry and the First Canadian Infantry Brigade in Calgary. He also served on UN peacekeeping assignments and NATO duties in Europe.
In 1971 he was promoted to Lieutenant-General and from 1973 until 1975 he commanded the Canadian army. A series of larger appointments in Ottawa afforded Stan an opportunity to observe closely the operation of Canada's government and its departments.
Following a distinguished military career, he joined the Mannix organization in Calgary in July 1975.
His transition to the business world was both swift and successful. In just over six months he became president of the Loram Group engaged in national and international activities, in heavy construction, oil and gas, coal, engineering and manufacturing.
This private sector experience, with all of the driving forces of Alberta's complex economy, gave Stan invaluable knowledge and skill in developing policy for the west and for Canada.
To his private sector career, Stan brought the loyalty, leadership, sense of service and drive developed during an extensive military career.
In August 1989 he was nominated by the Reform Party of Canada to contest the election for senatorial selection in Alberta. On October 16, 1989 he was elected by a large margin, nearly double that of the votes of the next candidate. After a wait of nearly nine months the Prime Minister acceded to the wishes of the Alberta electorate and appointed Stan Waters to the Senate in June 1990.
I was here when Senator Stan came to Ottawa in June 1990 to be sworn in as Canada's first ever elected senator. How exciting it was to be part of that historical occasion. During Senator Waters' one year in the Senate I appreciated his deep knowledge and understanding on a wide variety of issues. What company and comfort he offered to me on a personal basis, as well as politically.
I will always remember Stan Waters' ram-rod straight, military fashion commanding respect from all he came in contact with. I will also always remember Stan whisking into my office, slumping, relaxed into a chair and saying: "Well, Deborah, what can we do for the nation today?"
Stan was honest, direct and took a no-nonsense approach to whatever had to be done. He never compromised his beliefs.
I was fortunate to know Stan on a very personal basis. We shared a platform often. We travelled together and ate supper together while here in Ottawa. He was genuinely concerned about me as a person and would jump to my defence on any issue as a father would guard his daughter.
In closing, my life has been enriched by knowing Stan Waters. He was a great proponent of Senate reform, and I was pleased to see the government put Senate reform on the constitutional table before his death. That is a tribute to him as a pioneer in the Senate reform movement.
Canada has lost a great statesman. To Stan's wife, Barbara, his children Claudia, Mark, Virginia, Caroline and their families, I want to say thank you for sharing Stan with ail of us.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my party, we wish to associate ourselves with the regrets already expressed at the passing of Senator Waters.
Stanley Waters led an exemplary and straightforward life with strong convictions, and he had the determination to pursue those convictions.
He joined the army during World War II and he worked his way up rank by rank to the very top, holding the rank of Lieutenant-General, Commanding Officer of the army contingent of the Canadian Forces at retirement.
He then turned to the world of business, working as a general manager of the well respected Mannix group for almost 15 years.
He held strong political views and, even though we in this party do not share all of them, we admired him for his tenacity and determination in pursuing them.
Among his views that we do share is the desirability of an elected Senate. When the opportunity arose for him to contest an election for the Senate he had the strength of character not only to contest and to win that election but to wait patiently for the many months that it took the Government of Canada to accept the verdict of the people.
September 26, 1991

It is unfortunate that Senator Waters' health prevented him from serving longer in the Senate where he was an active spokesperson for a point of view somewhat different from the others found in the Upper Chamber.
We want to join with our colleagues in expressing our deepest sympathies to Mrs. Waters, their daughters and their son at this most difficult time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to join with the hon. member for Beaver River and the House leader of the Liberal Party in this tribute to the late Senator Stan Waters.
I knew Stan for a number of years. I basically knew him when he arrived in Calgary after retirement from the army and had met him prior to that when he was still serving in the army. He was an outstanding Canadian. Of that there is no doubt. His military service record established that clearly. He was a member of the famous Devil's Brigade, which was the subject of a movie. The Devil's Brigade was so-named by the Germans who found this Canadian-American group pretty fearsome. He rose to become the commander of the army, and upon retirement moved to Calgary and took a senior position with the Mannix group of companies. Another graduate of the Mannix group of companies was Peter Lougheed. That company seems to turn out politically active people.
Stan was an ally and a supporter for most of his politically active life. We differed in the last couple of years of his life but never about the question of the value of an elected Senate. In that regard his efforts are applauded and were a valuable contribution to the evolution of the constitutional structure of this country.
I too would like to join with other members of this House in offering our condolences to his wife and children, and say to them that in this difficult period they at least have the comfort of knowing that their husband and father was an outstanding Canadian who gave tremendously to this country.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to extend the condolences of the New Democratic Party caucus to the family and friends of Senator Stan Waters. Like most Albertans and the
Business of the House
overwhelming majority of Canadians I did not know Stan Waters but I sure as heck knew of him.
Stan was one of those giants whom occasionally Alberta-and other areas of the country but Alberta in particular-seems to produce: a person of monumental integrity, granitic determination with a dedication to what he thought was the right thing to do, which was sufficient to help him past virtually all obstacles. In this he exemplified what is best in the Albertan and the Canadian spirit.
We have all lost a champion with the death of Stan Waters. However, I am certain that his legacy will live far beyond him and stand Canadians in good stead for decades to come.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to say that Senator Waters, whom I knew for about ten years, was always a person who was compassionate, approachable and caring. I would like to express my deepest sympathies to Mrs. Waters and the family and all of the grandchildren.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the people of Calgary Northeast I wish to express our deepest sympathy to the Waters family. We all knew Stan as a strong committed man of principles, a man who will take his place in history as one who contributed to raising the awareness of all Canadians about the undemocratic powers of some of our federal institutions.
General Waters represented Albertans with great dignity. We are especially proud of his contribution to political change and his place in history as Canada's first elected senator. He will be remembered as a great Canadian.
So that the House knows where we are proceeding next, I am going to take the usual Thursday afternoon question, and then I have a question of privilege which I must hear.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

subsubtopic: ACCESS TO THE DOCUMENT OUTLINING CONSTITUTIONAL PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been a member of the House of Commons for 12 years, and during that time, my interest has been, above all, the debate on the Constitution.
As an observer, I have attended all federal-provincial conferences on the Constitution, and I have always taken my duties and responsibilities as an elected representative very seriously. A few days ago, Mr. Speaker, a document was tabled in the House, a document said to be the most important one in this session, considering the future of relations between Quebec and Ottawa, whatever form that will take.
Mr. Speaker, I heard today-and this is why I wish to raise a question of privilege-I heard today that I, as an elected representative, was given access to this document at 10 a.m. on Tbesday, when the Prime Minister rose in the House. I also heard that Mr. Paul Desmarais, Mr. Roger D. Landry, The Globe and Mail and others who were not elected by anyone and whose only qualification is that they have either influence or a lot of money, were given access to this document, directly by the Prime Minister, sometime on Monday.
Mr. Speaker, I can hardly find words to express this affront to Parliament and to the people who elected me. How can people elected to represent 75,000 or 80,000 people, with a mandate to deal with issues that concern the future of our country, be ignored in this way and given this information at the last minute? Landry prevented me from being able to react as quickly as all members who had access, or the party leaders. According to my information, only the party leaders had a briefing.
