speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we had a brief intermission, we were talking about Bill C-19 relating to the Bank Act. I was talking generally about why we as a party are not in favour of this act but are in favour of allowing banks to market and sell insurance policies. I was supporting myself and my party in this position through the experience of the Quebec caisse populaires which have been doing it for so many years.
I have talked to some of my colleagues on the Liberal side as well as the Conservative side, and one of the things we do know about caisse populaires is that in marketing insurance the satisfaction of customers can vary depending on how the caisse populaire operates. Once again, because caisse populaires are responsible to their owners who are the people in the community, there can be some caisse populaires perhaps being more responsible and more competitive than others. I am willing to grant my colleagues that.
The important difference between what the caisse populaires do and what the banks would do if they

September 26, 1991
Government Orders
became owners-and that is the key word-of insurance companies is that the banks would not necessarily be responsible to their communities. They would be responsible to their shareholders. Insurance companies would not be responsible to their communities per se but to their shareholders which would be the banks.
It must be understood that this is not a position which is anti-corporation. It is not a position which is partisan or is anti-bank. What we are trying to be is pro-consumer. We want to see competition. We want to see the banks get in there and market insurance as the caisse populaires have done because we believe, as with the caisse populaires as I said before, this would bring about competition, competitive rates, competitive services, and at the same time employees would not lose their jobs. As a matter of fact in Quebec it has done veiy well, particularly from 1985 to 1991.
I just wanted to explain why we are in favour of allowing the banks to market insurance plans but not becoming owners of insurance companies.
I would just like to mention one last thing for those of us in this House who are from the prairies, who have seen the kind-heartedness of the banks when it comes to farmers who cannot pay their mortgages. I am concerned about what happened with banks owning insurance companies and farmers or consumers not being able to pay their insurance premiums. What would happen? What power could be brought to bear?
I really think that where banks and co-operatives primarily deal as marketers that augments competition and at the same time it protects consumers. That is why our party, which wants to maximize consumer protection, is in favour of that aspect.
I want to bring to the attention of the House the point about abuse of power. I am concerned about the abuse of power as we give more power to the banks. As a consumer advocate, I have seen it work in the sense of being veiy much against the consumer interest.
I mentioned a very interesting Supreme Court case of Houle v. Banque nationale du Canada. The judgment is in French and English and it shows how the banks with the power they have can actually put a small business owner into bankruptcy. I was referring to the Belanger-Cam-peau Commission where the co-chairman was actually the head of the Banque nationale du Canada and he objected very strenuously to my presentation of a brief in
which I criticized the Banque nationale du Canada, referring to the Houle v. the Banque nationale du Canada decision in the Supreme Court of Canada. He had said that was not a proper complaint to make. I think it is.
Mr. Belanger referred to the fact that there is already a lot of protection for consumers. No matter what powers we give the banks today or with the passage of this legislation consumers will have a complaint mechanism. That is true. There is theory and there is reality. The reality is that there is not all that much protection.
Who protected them? I have a report here which is very interesting. It is actually a citation from a book called The Economics of Government Regulation, Theory and Canadian Practice. It is written by John C. Strick, and it is very interesting.
It says: "The increasing number of failures of financial institutions during the 1980s and the difficulties incurred by others brought the effectiveness of these early warning systems and the regulation of financial institutions into question. Mismatched assets and liabilities, the questionable quality of loans and lack of diversification were among the causes of failures of trust companies and the failure of the Northland Bank and the Canadian Commercial Bank."
I am worried about what little power we really do have over the banks as far as their practices are concerned, and I agree with my hon. colleague from Nickel Belt when he said: "Let's keep them in their respective cages. Let's give them the limited powers they have. Let bankers be bankers."
I think the central thing is that we should look at what happened with American Express. I wrote a letter to the president of American Express more than a month ago. I have not received a response. The letter that I sent to him was referring to restaurant owners of Quebec who found out that the 5 per cent that they were asked to pay American Express for clients to use their credit cards was exactly double that which restaurant owners have to pay in the United States.
They thought it was unfair. They are boycotting American Express in my province. I just asked the president of American Express to explain to me why we have this anomaly, and I have yet to receive a reply. TMk about complaint mechanisms.
September 26, 1991

When a member of Parliament cannot get a reply, who can?
In summation, I want to talk about American Express and interest rates.
Take a look at the lowering of interest rates that we all, as parliamentarians, have seen and that the other side has often reminded us of. I appreciate that reminder from the government side, but every time I see my statement from Visa or the other companies, I see the interest rates not going down appreciably, but staying the same.
What is our complaint mechanism? We have none. What is the social responsibility of the banks? I do not think it is very large in their estimation. What about the possibility of getting the banks to be socially responsible in bringing down their interest rates? If we are talking about 21 per cent, that is only the middle ground. Some of the interest rates are as high as 28 per cent. That is not socially responsible.
I referred to my hon. colleague from Nickel Belt. He presented a private members' bill trying to create a ceiling so that there will be only a certain number of percentage points above the general rate. That has not been dealt with but I think it is an interesting idea.
The summation is this. Our party is in favour of competition. We are in favour of giving the banks more diversification because through Third World loan problems, through the recession, banks need some protection, perhaps through diversification. We are not in favour of allowing the banks to become so globalized, such a predator or awesome creature that we all get eaten alive.

September 26, 1991

As a result of a mistake made by the company in crediting the wrong amount, an amount other than what was written on my cheque when I paid the account, I was threatened and harassed. Finally we got it straightened out. To this day I do not know whether that experience is a blemish on my credit rating or not.
I was shocked and very, very upset when my new card came about three months ago -and because I am of Scottish ancestry I hate to pay for something I do not need-I decided that I was going to cut it up and send it back and ask to have my account closed.
The company charges $55 for membership. If we do not use the card, cut it up, and send it back. Naturally the account should be closed and that $55 should be written off.
Elowever, I received a notice the next month that I owed $55. Just yesterday, I received a notice saying that my account was going to be cancelled unless I paid that $55, in spite of the fact that I notified the company in writing, cut up the card and sent it back to them.
How do you deal with a company like that? The reason I am talking about this today is because this morning I wrote them a letter and sent it by registered mail explaining these details. Tomorrow morning I am going to send them another letter and include a copy of Hansard. We will see what action that brings.
I took part in the debate on the amendments to the last Bank Act back in the early 1980s and I welcome the opportunity to participate in the second reading debate on Bills C-19 and C-28.1 want to make it very clear that the Liberal Party of Canada supports in principle this new legislation.
The banking and insurance industries have been waiting a long time for this new legislation and, while our party has some concerns about both bills, we will not stand in the way of their passing. We will seek to have our concerns addressed when the bills go back to committee.
I just want to touch on a few of those concerns, the concerns that I as a farmer have, and which I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you must have as you represent a riding not unlike the one I represent.
I am very concerned because over the last several years our farm industry has been the subject of attack
Government Orders
from various sectors. We have been the subject of an attack that accused our marketing systems of ripping off the consumer.
I conducted a study this summer. I did not take any time off my job as a parliamentarian, but I conducted a major study, with the assistance of my competent staff: Nick Heisler, my research assistant, and Susan Mogen-sen and Sue Richardson. We called this study "Compare the Share". One of the things shown very clearly, these figures are from Statistics Canada or Agriculture Canada, on a graph-and this is an illustrated study, it is very easy to read-is that farm input prices go up across the graph while income figures go the other way.
No business can survive with that sort of thing happening. A lot of those increases in inputs was a result of interest rates. There is a big difference between the interest rates in Canada and those in the U.S. There is also a big difference between the fuel prices in Canada and the U.S. However, some of the shockers-and they are all in this study-include that the producer price for milk went up by 19 cents a litre in the last 10 years, well below the rate of inflation, while the price between the producer and the consumer increased by 73 cents a litre, or 97 per cent. That is an increase in the inflation rate of 9.7 per cent per year, and that is not acceptable.
For cheese, the producer price increased by $1.53 per kilogram while the spread between the cheese factory and the consumer increased by $5.34 per kilogram, an increase of 86.4 per cent. Again, double the level of inflation.
For chicken, the processor-retail spread increased by $2.20 per kilogram, an increase of 87 per cent, while the producer price increased by 28 cents per kilogram. At the same time as com prices in Ontario declined over the last 10 years, the consumer price of com flakes increased by 97 per cent. The price of wheat to the farmer declined in the last 10 years while the retail price of sweet cookies increased by 111 per cent, solid cookies by 132 per cent, whole wheat cereals by 192.6 per cent and crackers by 235 per cent.
During this whole time, we experienced a period of high interest rates, which were raised to counteract inflation, to bring down inflation; interest rates which created hardship for countless Canadian people, particularly primary producers.

September 26, 1991
Government Orders
We keep hearing the buzz word "competitiveness", that we have to be more competitive to compete in the global market. Yet, we see the devastation in our communities in close proximity to the U.S. border caused by cross-border shopping. The fact of the matter remains that, due to the concentration of the food industry, after the food leaves the processor there are increases in the price of these food products several times the rate of inflation, and they are ignored by government.
Why didn't the Governor of the Bank of Canada look into this cause of inflation? Where has he been? I keep thinking of the bird that flew the coop. Why was he not monitoring this increase, and where was the Bureau of Competition? We know where some of them were, they were criticizing our farm producers and telling us we had to be more competitive and attacking our marketing board systems, which are the most sophisticated systems in the world.
This study completely vindicates our farm marketing board systems. They have provided food to the Canadian consumer, high quality fopd at very reasonable prices. Yet, the consumer has been ripped off after the food has left the processor.
I am concentrating on the concentration in the marketplace. If this concentration is allowed to continue it is going to create more hardship for other sectors of society.
This is happening. We know the Minister of Agriculture has funded the Canadian Consumers Association to do a study of marketing boards, a study based on false assumptions. Why was there not an examination done of the concentration in the corporate sector? I want to emphasize that point. One of the retail food chains in western Canada-where there is a population of somewhere between 7.5 million people and 8.5 million people-serving the area from Thunder Bay west to the Pacific coast sent $545 million in dividends back to the parent company in the United States last year. How can we have it both ways, telling our own people that we have to be more competitive when $545 million is leaving this country in the form of dividends? It doesn't add up.
The Canadian farmer has to have a fair share of the consumer's food dollar or he will not survive.
I am deeply concerned about the concentration of power in the corporate sector. I fear that this will become a government of corporate decision. Who will provide the counterbalance to the marketplace if this concentration continues? Until now, in the rural sector, in the farm sector, those marketing boards provided that counterbalance to the marketplace. If they are traded away at GATT, where is that counterbalance going to come from?
It was just a year ago that the Minister for International Trade at the time, now the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, chastized the Minister of Agriculture for the $8.8 billion worth of subsidies to farmers, $2.2 billion of that going to Canadian dairy farmers. That was not a subsidy. Their actual subsidy was $267 million. You know that, Mr. Speaker.
The government was using an aggregate measure of support, which was a concocted figure. It took the difference between what American fanners received for milk and what Canadians received for milk and called that a $2.2 billion subsidy, completely ignoring the fact that our input costs are 25 per cent higher on this side of the border. If that is a subsidy to our Canadian dairy producers, then I maintain that the fact that our interest rates in Canada are 25 per cent higher than those in the United States must be considered a subsidy to the banks. If it is sauce for the goose it is sauce for the gander. I hope this government realizes that before it starts giving away the store at the GATT negotiations coming up in the near future.
I fear the same thing is going to happen with the financial institutions.
I just want to make a quote from a news article. It is an editorial that says:
The growing monopolistic control of agribusiness and food companies continues. Our federal government has not only allowed this growing concentration but has often encouraged it. We believe this concentration of agricultural and food enterprises is depressing farm commodity prices and depressing our economic recovery. About six corporations dominate the grain business. The big three control 80 per cent of the fed beef business and four or five of these companies also dominate the poultry and hog business. Some of the biggest companies own cattle feed yards, plus hog raising and poultry raising facilities. They are grain traders, grain exporters, feed manufacturers and food processors. We still "wonder" because strange things are happening. Ibtal supplies of grains and beans are at the lowest levels in 30 years yet prices continue at record lows. During the past four weeks the bottom has fallen out of the cattle
September 26, 1991

markets. Meat packers say prices are lower because USDA reports show there is a glut of fat cattle in the feedlots.
Mr. Speaker, this must sound familiar to you because you are a farmer yourself, but that is an editorial out of The Thumb Farm News in the State of Michigan. I submit that the same thing is going to happen in Canada if this continues.
I also want to quote from another article in another issue of the same paper. The headline is "Feeding a hungry world from an empty shelf". I just want to say that this article points out very clearly that the supplies of grain and com in the U.S. at the present time are at very, very low levels. It says:
The only meaningful supply of surplus food is in Western Europe and Canada. We are approaching our fall harvest with indications we'll have a reduced com and bean harvest-.This in turn could reduce future milk, meat and poultry production. Meanwhile U.S. farm prices, adjusted to 1982 dollars, are the lowest in history and showing little signs of increasing.

This ties in with our Canadian farm income. When I look at the farm debt structure in Canada, I shudder. This industry cannot continue under current conditions and if this government trades away our dairy and poultry sector at GATT, you will see a tremendous erosion of assets immediately. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I want to take this House back and try to reconstruct as best I can from the facts we have on record a story which I believe is sordid and which requires rectification.
It began some time in mid-1986. A company by the name of 158792 Canada Limited with its head office at 101 McNab Street, Markham, Ontario applied for a bank licence. This was not an ordinary bank licence in Canada but a licence as a Schedule B bank, a foreign bank coming into Canada.
Many foreign bank licences had been granted under the normal provisions of the law, a law which had been opened up very widely since 1980. In the ordinary course of events these banks were automatically granted their charters and their rights to do business in Canada. It was part of the policy of the previous government and this government.
However, something happened. The application for this bank licence became stalled. For 27 months our officials here in Ottawa sat on this application and would not grant it.
Let us go . forward a couple of years. In the 1988 election, and the election campaign that took place on a very heated basis in 1980, there were some dramatic swings in the polls and the major issue facing Canadians was that of free trade. Canadians can legitimately be for or against free trade and were at that time because it was a major issue.
One thing that happened which I think is unusual in Canadian election history is that during the latter parts of that election campaign massive funds and massive lobbying started to pour in to Canada and smear campaigns were all over the television and the newspapers.
Who was launching this campaign? There was a massively financed campaign in the United States in support of free trade led by Mr. James Robinson and Mr. Ross Johnson. Mr. James Robinson is the president of American Express and Mr. Robinson, a director of American Express, was with J. R. Nabisco.
In Canada a lobby spearheaded by the Business Council on National Issues, whose chairman was David Culver, led the campaign for free trade. Is it any coincidence that Mr. David Culver was also a director of American Express U.S.? What we had on election day was not only the victory of the Conservative government which we all know about. Many Canadians, most people in Canada, did not vote for free trade. However, some-

Government Orders
thing happened on November 21, election day, apart from the electoral results. An Order in Council was passed.
Elow could the Clerk of the Privy Council scurry around on election day in bad weather and get the signatures of three cabinet ministers on a particular Order in Council? This Order in Council passed November 21, 1988, election day, was an Order in Council to create the Amex Bank of Canada.
On December 17, 1988, published in the Globe and Mail-and that was a Saturday just before Christmas- was a small ad saying that 158792 Canada Limited intended to apply for letters patent in order to become Amex Bank of Canada.
The member for York Centre realized in January 1989 what was happening and called for an inquiry. On February 1, 1989 I raised this issue publicly, asking for full details. On February 3, the Minister of Finance-I do not know whether it was out of embarrassment or out of a sense of what he thought was justice, I certainly thought it was the proper thing to say at the time- said to Canadians through this House: "We will not grant letters patent to Amex Bank Limited until such time as all of the financial legislation dealing with the banks is in place". It had been on the table for many years but the government was working to bring it to a head.
Why did we object vehemently to this indication that American Express would be able to carry on business in Canada as a bank at this particular time? Very briefly, American Express was in breach of five out of nine of the government's own guidelines for the admission of foreign banks to Canada. That is why the competent members of the bureaucracy had sat on this application for over two years and had not allowed it to go through. Five out of the nine guidelines of this government were breached the moment Amex Bank Limited was entitled to carry on business in Canada.
This was unprecedented. No wonder the minister was embarrassed and said: "We will give you the legislation before they have a chance to carry on their banking business". This was not to be.
Later, in spring 1989, we were told "No, we cannot wait for the bank legislation to come down. It is too urgent that American Express be granted its licence to do business in Canada". Finally, on April 25, 1990, the
government bit the bullet-I am sure there were members of that government who did not want to have to bite that bullet-and issued the letters patent to American Express giving it the right to carry on the banking business in Canada in breach of five of the government's nine guidelines, which had not been changed. This was opposed by the Canadian Banking Association and by every person in Canada who believes that no person should be above the law.
Why this unseemly haste? Why did the government have to put the cart before the horse to grant privileges to a company. Did it have something to do with the free trade deal and the leadership shown by American Express both in Canada and in the United States in supporting the free trade deal? They are entitled to do that. Everyone is entitled to fight openly for the policies they want to see for Canada, but it is not fair for a government to give special privileges and break its own guidelines to anyone, regardless of how close they are as political cronies.
In this Bank Act amendment what do we see dealing with this particular issue, American Express. We see that the government has not even dealt properly with the issue at hand. It has tried retroactively to change the guidelines for the admission of foreign banks. It says: "You do not have to be a bank in your home jurisdiction. We will expand that. We will expand it to cover companies such as American Express".
American Express was not a bank in its home jurisdiction, the United States, nor was it regulated as a bank in its home jurisdiction of the United States. So what has the government done? It has said that pretty well any financial institution from the United States or abroad can come into Canada.
In the guidelines the minister brought down last fall for the reform of federal financial institutions, it said that schedule II bank designations would be expanded to include non-banks owned by widely regulated financial institutions that are not themselves banks.
The key phrase was "regulated financial institutions". Do we find that phrase "regulated financial institutions" in the new guidelines to deal with this type of situation? No, the government has taken out the word "regulated". So any type of so-called financial institution now has the
September 26, 1991

privilege to sweep through the door as a result of the legislation this government is attempting to pass to justify retroactively its privileged treatment of American Express. Is this good for Canada's financial institutions and for our financial climate? It creates a great deal of uncertainty.
Does it mean that institutions such as Ford Credit, Chrysler Credit, Sears, IBM and General Electric- which are huge financing institutions; they issue commercial paper and extend credit to the customers who buy their products-will be able to come into Canada to compete with our banks?
BCCI was a foreign bank that came into Canada. However, I believe there is some indication that maybe its ultimate owner was simply a non-bank holding company from Luxembourg.
Is it fair to impose upon bank regulators in Canada the obligation to supervise all of these foreign banks and the few that are Canadian? The vast multitude which are now doing business in Canada are foreign; over 60 of our banks are foreign. Is it fair to impose upon our bank regulators the necessity to regulate these and examine what they are doing in every other jurisdiction, in order to determine whether they are sound, whether they are obeying the laws, whether they are legal, and whether they are laundering money? No. We want at least to ensure, and the taxpayers of Canada want the right to ensure, that banks coming into Canada from abroad are regulated according to the high standards which we think are appropriate. In that way we will protect Canadian investors, Canadian users of the banks. That is right and fair. Why open this whole thing up?
That is not the only consideration. In the free trade agreement-and we did not see the final version in September-in the final version are contained some annexes. There is an annex B called "tourism services". Inserted in annex B, which extended free trade to various service industries, were tourism services including tourism related services of a financial nature. I would like to know who it was who lobbied the government to include tourism related services of a financial nature into the free trade deal at the last minute. Canadians have a right to know.
Government Orders
Was it one of the giants of international tourism? Was it a foreign firm? Why was it put in? Who was going to benefit from it? Why was it not included up front when these documents were being considered in September? Why was it slipped in, in November 1988?
Another problem we face in terms of the free trade deal with the United States is that our banks did not receive reciprocity with American banks. They did receive national treatment. That means that American banks coming into Canada can do as Canadian banks do here. American Express can also do in Canada some things that Canadian banks cannot do. It can sell all sorts of goods on its plastic. It has the ability to be in the tourism business. Do Canadian banks receive the same treatment in the United States as American Express does here? They do not.
Under the Glass-Steagall Act, Canadian banks cannot acquire U.S. securities firms. We did not get that right under the free trade agreement. American banks have privileges in Canada that Canadian banks do not have in the United States.
Another instance is the McFeddran Act. In the United States there are certain limitations on interstate branch banking. Canadian banks going into the United States are still subject to those restrictions. American banks coming into Canada are not subject to those branch banking restrictions.
We did not even get a fair trade for our Canadian banks. Not only were the laws of Canada breached to grant special privileges to American Express, but our own financial institutions are put at a competitive disadvantage.
The banks are asking Canadians to give them extended privileges: insurance, the ability to get into auto leasing, and many other things. These are privileges they have not been granted.
The banks have a point: "Why can't you give us at least the same privileges you are prepared to give to American Express? Why should we be hamstrung as financial institutions?"
The bank serves two functions in Canada. One is as a service industry to help finance, as intermediaries of deposits from every one of us, investment and business and job creation.

Government Orders
They are a key tool to a dynamic, growing economy. Let us look at them as an industry on their own, the employment and the innovations they are bringing, the technological changes and what they can do for our GNP, both in Canada and through their international banking operations.
When the banks come to the House of Commons and say to government "we want more privileges", how can this government with clean hands say: "No, we will not give them to you but we were happy to give them to American Express"?
I was hoping that the bank legislation would have dealt with this issue. I would hope that the committee would have a full opportunity to hear officials from American Express, the government and our bureaucrats as to why they held up this application for some 24 to 27 months.
I believe that this is an issue which needs a full airing, and I believe it is critical to restore confidence in a non-partisan operation of all our laws to all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in this debate which is a very important one because it is only once every 10 years that we really get to take a broad view of the banking system in this country and how it operates.
I guess I found it ironic that I was on my way flying to Ottawa to speak on a bill on banking and I needed to drive from Prince Albert to Saskatoon to catch the plane. I stopped in my home town of Laird, Saskatchewan to see my parents who had just finished harvesting. They are still farming at 75 years of age because it is not profitable for young fanners to get started. My parents informed me they were quite distressed that the bank in Laird, Saskatchewan was closing, a bank that had been there I think since 1912 or 1914.
In my mind that serves as the backdrop as to what I wanted to say about this legislation. As with so much of the legislation that we see here, this legislation is directed at something that might solve a problem and might be helpful in inner Canada but might well be a total disaster again in what might be termed outer Canada. I want to give credit to the hon. member for Edmonton Southeast for introducing the terms inner and outer Canada. I think they describe things very well.

Government Orders
When it comes to inner Canada perhaps there is an argument that can be made for the kind of things we are seeing in this bill: the deregulation, the allowing of different kinds of financial institutions to merge and carry on businesses and partnerships, and so on. Perhaps there is an element of truth in the fact that in order for Canadian financial institutions to compete at the global level, to be there in Geneva, Paris, Stockholm, Tokyo, and wherever you all have to be in order to function at that level of finance, we need bigger institutions to be able to play the game at that level.
What we are in danger of creating here is what the hon. member for Nickel Belt described today as a whole cast of uncontrolled sumo wrestlers. These beings that are being created here are so huge that just the physical size of them makes them virtually impossible to regulate. It makes it virtually impossible to bring them under any kind of public interest kind of umbrella.
Maybe that makes sense for the wheelers and dealers in Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal and those people who feel that the free trade deal that we have already signed and perhaps the free trade deal with Mexico is a bonanza for them and the people they represent as shareholders and so on. I do not represent those kinds of people so I have not had the opportunity to converse with them personally, but I know what people think about the banking system in outer Canada.
In outer Canada the banking system is viewed quite differently, Mr. Speaker, as you know, representing a rural constituency yourself. Small business people, main street people, abhor many of the practices that the banks carry out, particularly in smaller communities. When I talk to the business community in Prince Albert, a city of 35,000,1 hear nothing but a litany of tales about lines of credit being cut off, about loans being unreasonably turned down even for very worth-while enterprises by well established companies, but it seems that when somebody writes a stoiy in Toronto that says Saskatchewan is in trouble, all of a sudden all the money dries up in Saskatchewan. That is just a common pattern that has been happening to our province at least for the last number of years.
This fact is more than amply demonstrated in the surveys that we as members get from independent
business organizations that rank banking and banking services very low as far as helping them to do business.
Then we have the whole perception of the banking system in rural Canada. To rural Canada nowadays the banking system means foreclosure. It means being taking to court by the banks. What I am concerned about is that not only is the government not intervening in any meaningful way to enhance the financial situation of farmers, but in a situation where these financial institutions are all combining and forming conglomerates you could well end up getting your farm seized or machinery seized because you have not paid an insurance bill, for example. It will vastly widen the scope of what banks are able to do to the farmer and other consumers and business people because of the inter-relationships that will exist.
I might add also that this is made even worse by the fact that instead of having the stable agriculture system we once had, we have moved to increasing instability. This is not only because of the international factors but because we have got into the political ad hoc mode of supporting agriculture so that farmers have to go to the banker and try to convince them that yes there is an election coming in Saskatchewan and the federal government will likely be coming up with some money in order to get a loan. That is the kind of situation that we place the farm population in.
Another aspect of outer Canada that I would like to raise in this debate is that facing frontier Canada. Part of my constituency includes virtually all the northern half of Saskatchewan which is made up of 43 isolated communities in the forest, many of them Indian communities, mining communities and so on. There are a lot of communities spread out across Canada that are much like that.
Over the years the banking system has made untold billions of dollars out of those communities. There have been hundreds of millions of dollars in wealth generated by the mines, forests and fishing. Those banks have never seen a responsibility to return any part of that to those communities in terms of service. There are only three banking institutions in the north half of Saskatchewan. That means business people there are sometimes a two, three or four hour drive, sometimes even a flight away from a banking institution to do any banking. People who want to establish a line of credit simply
September 26, 1991

cannot because banks will not recognize anyone more than 50 miles away as being in their trading area.
We have a banking system that makes untold billions of dollars out of frontier areas but does not even show up to provide a service. I would like to comment on some breakthroughs being made in that area by peoples' own initiatives. I am speaking now of the major initiative being launched by Arctic co-operatives to develop credit unions in the Northwest Territories and also in my own constituency. The Buffalo Narrows Credit Unions will for the first time supply a banking service to northwest Saskatchewan.
My question comes out of this. We are now talking about the banking system in this country and it is clearly not working. We are seeing another retreat on another front that pertains to exactly the same question. That is the question that was raised in Question Period today by our leader, the member for Yukon, that is the move by this government to restrict the functions of the Bank of Canada. They are proposing to restrict the functions of the Bank of Canada to controlling inflation, to keeping inflation at zero per cent. That is a vast diminution in the role of the Bank of Canada.
Explicitly in the past the Bank of Canada had to pay attention to things like growth, unemployment and providing service to the regions. That is not in the Bank of Canada's mandate any more. I am asking in this legislation if we are not going to do it through private sector banking or through the Bank of Canada, what kind of mechanism do we have in this country to ensure that capital goes to the places where it is needed and to provide services some place other than where the big shots feel they can make some money? That question is fundamentally unanswered, and I think my basic criticism of this bill is that it is far too narrow in how it views the banking system.
In closing, my time is getting short. I would like to make some mention of what I think is a positive aspect of this legislation, and that is the changes to the Co-operative Credit Associations Act. The credit union system is a success story and does hold hope for outer Canada and for all those Canadians that will be marginalized in the post-free trade world.

There are about 2,600 credit unions in this country with 9 million members. Over one-third of Canadians are members of credit unions. They have assets of approximately $69 billion in this country. They are a significant institution already. With this legislation I have to give the government, the finance committee and others credit. They have given the credit union movement some new tools whereby it can get into commercial lending and can have some of the same powers and advantages that trust companies have. It is going to be able to raise capital from outside its membership base in order to be competitive.
I believe these are steps forward. It will also make it possible for the credit union system to better finance the rest of the co-op movement in providing services and economic hope to many of the regions of this country.
With that and recognizing the time, I would just like to say that the government has taken one step forward in a very important area, and that is the area of ensuring that credit unions and co-operatives can play their legitimate roles.
However, on the other hand we are still continuing the headlong retreat from the kind of financial system and the kind of economic structure in this country that will allow each Canadian to know that this country's economy is there to serve them and not to just serve the wealthy and the powerful.

INCOME TAX QUARTERLY INSTALMENTS Mr. John Harvard (Winnipeg St. James) moved
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of changing the collection of income tax as it affects citizens whose income is not taxed at source so that senior citizens who are required to pay income tax in four quarterly instalments will be obligated to pay only one annual instalment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I deem it a privilege to have initiated this motion and I am honoured to lead off today's debate.

September 26, 1991
Private Members' Business
The senior citizens of this country are being denied a choice I think they deserve. They have worked long and hard for retirement and they deserve the option of not paying income tax in quarterly instalments. Senior citizens and self-employed individuals owing more than $1,000 in income tax must pay quarterly instalments of their estimated annual income tax. Payment dates must be strictly adhered to and estimates of the next year's income must be reliable. That is the law.
I was drawn to this issue by a number of senior citizens in my riding who, like thousands of other Canadian seniors, have miscalculated their income tax or accidentally or inadvertently missed a payment date.
When this happens the government slaps huge interest charges on the late payment. Instead of giving them the benefit of the doubt, Revenue Canada automatically assumes that these seniors are maliciously trying to withhold taxes and defraud the government.
The vast majority of Canadians do not ever have to worry about missing a tax payment. It is simply taken off every one of our paycheques. But most seniors do not have that luxury. Like the self-employed they have to do the calculating themselves.
The government would like everybody to pay income tax on the weekly or bi-weekly schedule because ideally income tax should be paid as income is earned.
On the face of it, quarterly instalments sound like a fair compromise between bi-weekly payments and an annual lump sum payment. But for many members of our society this compromise simply is not working. I will bring forward testimony to that effect in a few minutes.
The government justifies mandatory quarterly instalments by claiming that allowing an annual lump sum payment would be like giving seniors loans in the amount of the tax payable. In theory this is true but in practice many seniors end up actually lending the government money between tax instalments.
Often seniors will overestimate and hence overpay the government because they are unable to guess how much income they will be earning.
The other justification the government uses to support mandatory instalments is that it is trying to help Canadian seniors avoid possible budgeting problems.
Pardon my cynicism, Mr. Speaker, but I doubt many Canadians appreciate this government giving out financial advice. We hardly need to treat retired Canadians like adolescents. The majority of our seniors have been paying income tax for decades, and they have learned how to budget after living through the depression and several recessions.
Research has shown that seniors can generally be characterized as economy conscious and they are less likely to use credit cards. This is hardly an age group that takes the attitude buy now, pay later. They could probably teach this government a thing or two. Enough has already been taken away from our seniors. They face old age security clawbacks, a crumbling health care system and caps on the funding of other social programs.
Our country has not prepared itself for an aging society. We often treat the elderly as a burden, not as an asset, and then every three months we turn around and tell them to pay up. I think we are a bit callous.
It certainly would not hurt this House to demonstrate a little bit of compassion and flexibility for once. Yes, we would be making an exception for one segment of our society, but this is not a case of benefiting one segment while depriving another. All Canadians could eventually benefit from this motion.
I cannot believe that the option of paying taxes at one time would really be too expensive for the government. As it is, an army of Revenue Canada employees must be paid to assess and reassess every tax instalment a senior citizen makes. Even retired accountants must have a difficult time accurately predicting every penny they will earn in the coming year. The single payment option could eliminate this guess work on the part of the senior and eliminate the need for ongoing scrutiny of his or her account at Revenue Canada.
The government might claim that estimating income should not be difficult for a senior citizen; after all they are usually retired so their income should not change much from one year to another. On paper this should hold true and it probably works out fine for many seniors, I will grant you that, but there are plenty of seniors who do not have straightforward incomes. They have investments that change from year to year. They
September 26, 1991

have part-time jobs and they can have enormous differences in medical deductions from year to year.
To top it all off, if they do accidentally pay less than they owe, they are not told so. They are simply told to pay the difference with interest-I underline that, with interest. No reminder, no statement showing where they erred; just give us the interest you owe us. No business in this country treats its customers like that. We are given 30 or 60 days to pay our bills. We are told in advance how much we will owe if we do not pay on time.
The government may justify this by saying that our seniors should know how much to pay and when to pay it because they are the ones who calculated the instalments in the first place. This argument lacks one crucial aspect, though. It does not take into account the fact that all of us, all of us, are likely to get a little confused and a little forgetful when we reach a certain age. This is not something that we should be punished for. It is simply a fact of life with many older citizens and it is something the government should learn to work around.
Because of quarterly instalments, it is very common to see people paying tax on income they have never seen. A number of my constituents have told me that although their Canada Savings Bonds and other investments do not mature until the fall, they are still forced to pay tax on them in the month of March.
One woman wrote: "Paying quarterly means paying on income I have not yet received. Thus, I am losing interest on money paid in advance while Revenue Canada collects interest on it. This to me is the same as my paying double interest".
Today's seniors grew up without the social programs that our young people now take for granted. Seniors do not blithely take what they can get from the government. Often they are too proud to ask for the services they deserve. On the other hand, they tend to give to this country. They volunteer. They fight hard on behalf of other groups and they pay their taxes.
It is rare that this Parliament has the chance to give something back to the people of Canada. So much of our time is spent debating policies that take things away from
Private Members' Business
Canadians. For once we can do the right thing and make the lives of some senior citizens just a little easier.
If we can admit that the present system has failed many seniors, then we are on the right track. If we can save a few people from the headaches and confusion caused by quarterly income tax payments, then I believe we have succeeded.
I brought the motion to the attention of my constituents several months ago. I have received a lot of mail on this issue. With the Chair's indulgence, I would like to enter into the parliamentary record portions of letters I have received on this issue in support of seniors and in support of this proposed tax change.
Here is a copy of a letter I received. It went to Revenue Canada. A portion of it states:
"Enclosed you will find cheques totally $1,099.55. The cheque for $162.89 is so-called instalment interest which you have the unmitigated gall to charge me. The cheque for $936.66 covers two instalments of $468.33 for March 15, 1991 and June 15, 1991.
I am a senior citizen and for the many, many years that I have paid income tax, I have always paid in full on April 30, as required. I see no reason to change this procedure and I take exception to being told that I must pay quarterly or be charged interest".
That is a letter I received, dated June 7, sent to Revenue Canada and a copy of it was sent to me.
Here is another letter, dated July 30.1 will read just a portion of it:
"I have never been notified for my 1990 taxes that I should pay quarterly. My taxes for 1990 amounted to $6,046.38, of which $1,796.77 had already been deducted monthly from my pension, leaving $4,249.61 to be paid. I sent my cheque and Revenue Canada sent me a letter saying I did not owe anything.
Two months later I received a letter requesting $336.00, since I had not paid quarterly. I was told I should now pay $1,062 quarterly for my 1991 taxes. I have paid my $336 and I still maintain it is not fair".
Here is another letter I received from a constituent, dated July 25, 1991. The letter starts off:

"Five months to Christmas. I heartily agree with that proposal of seniors paying income tax once a year only. It is ridiculous for a senior person to pay tax in March on interest income received in November on Canada Savings Bonds".

This letter is dated August 6. "As a pensioner, I find it a real hassle each year trying to determine what tax I should pay to keep from being penalized. Your proposal is an excellent idea, and I wish you great success with the motion being put before Parliament."
