I have another letter, also from the month of July: "It certainly lifts my spirits to know you are doing your best for the elderly people in Canada. My stepmother is almost 80 years old and has served in the armed forces, and worked for the government until her retirement. She has never collected unemployment insurance and neither did my father. Of course, they paid into it.
Now, when my stepmother has a few years of leisure time, she is very worried about all the red tape involved in this quarterly tax payment."
This letter is dated August 22 and is from another senior citizen: "I am a senior citizen and I do not like to be told to pay every three months. I think once a year is all we should have to pay our taxes."
This letter is dated August 12. It is very short and to the point: "I am writing in support of your motion that would relieve pensioners from making compulsory quarterly income tax payments."
Here is one that is a little longer, and this will be the last letter that I will enter into the record. This letter writer entered into some calculation. It goes like this:
Dear Mr. Harvard:
Here is a classic case where the federal government is beating up on an 86 year old widow because she is about $200 short on paying 75 per cent of her taxable income and $549.44 short on paying the full amount.
This was the total tax payable for 1990: $2,398.19 This was the total tax credits for 1990: $1,848.75 Balance due and paid by cheque in April, 1991: $549.44 Interest and/or penalties on $549.44 was: $61.44
The writer continues:
Every month from January to November, 1990, through deductions from her late husband's pension cheques, $100 was paid and in December, 1990, $175 was paid for a total taxes paid of $1,275 for the 1990 taxation year. The interest or penalty was charged because the amount paid ($1,275) over the 12 months of 1990 was not 75 per cent of the taxable income that should have been paid on the net income and therefore a note from the Federal Government, I quote, "have charged you instalment interest as one or more of these payments was late or insufficient".
Another person may owe $5,000 to $10,000.00 at the end of the year but if they have paid 75 per cent of the taxable income in that year, then there is no interest or penalty charges on the $5,000 to $10,000.00 that was not paid in that tax year.
The problem can be solved by general averaging over the last three years with no cost to all taxpayers.
September 26, 1991

The writer of this letter finishes off by saying:
The Federal Government issue Old Age Pension cheques and C.P.P.
cheques every month by computer so they have the capability to
initiate deductions every month from those cheques. Thus seniors
remembering to write cheques four times a year would be eliminated.
I think those letters are a strong testimony that senior citizens in this country are in support of this motion and would welcome a change.
I would welcome support from Parliament on this motion and I think this is a chance for all of us to do something for Canadians who have worked so hard for their country. I know that they would welcome it.

Madam Speaker, I am glad that I happen to be on House duty this afternoon so that I became aware of the hon. member's motion because I myself have an interest in this subject.
I imagine that there probably is not a member of Parliament who has not received representations from people and, in particular, senior citizens, who have come with their concerns about the fact that they have been required to pay instalment interest on their taxes or instalments on their taxes and in many cases they have been unaware of the need to do this in the past because perhaps they just, for the first time, came over the limit requiring such payments, and have been caught and have been required to pay interest and penalties.
I have, therefore, been considering this question of what might be done to relieve this matter. I would like to offer some comments to the hon. member as to why I do not think his particular method of solving the problem would be a good one, but I also would like to give him a suggestion as an alternative that might achieve the same end that I have been considering and plan to put forward myself through the vehicle of my own committee, the finance committee, of which I am the chair. I am hoping that perhaps I can convince him that my method might be superior and perhaps he would agree.
I think that we have to understand why we have instalments in the first place. By and large, they are for people who earn money that is not taxed at source. People who earn a wage receive a monthly pay cheque, have their taxes deducted monthly or perhaps more often from their salary and automatically remit it to the government. For people who are self-employed and
Private Members' Business
receive income either through business that they are engaged in or through investments, interest, dividends and others, we require those people to pay income tax on a quarterly basis because to say that they only had to pay at the end of the year would be treating wage earners, who must pay monthly through their automatic deductions, unfairly.
In order to try to make it fair we say that people who earn income from interest and other sources should have to pay at least quarterly.
Over-all, I think that the theory is correct; for senior citizens or anyone else. I do not think we should necessarily identify senior citizens because there are many other people who may be required to pay instalments such as the operators of small business, just starting them up, where the amounts are relatively small.
The problem is that the $1,000 amount that requires people to pay instalment interest has been eroded by inflation to the point that a great number of people are being caught in the system who should not be in the system.
I would like to say to the hon. member that I think the objective here is to take a lot of people who are earning a relatively small amount of money, interest income or other income, and say: "You should not have to pay instalments, you should only have to pay once a year." I think that is proper. However, rather than apply a rule to all seniors that they do not have to pay instalments we should try to raise the limit from $1,000 of income tax owing to something more reasonable like a $10,000 annual income tax bill, at which point people will have to pay instalments.
That would be fair to everyone, seniors or people who are not seniors. It would also require that those earning investment income on amount-if someone has $1 million in the bank and is earning $100,000 a year- should have to pay instalment payments, just like wage earners have to pay monthly payments.
The difficulty in attempting to exempt a group of people is that it also exempts people who, some of us suggest, should be paying even more taxes. Those are people who are wealthy and perhaps have millions of dollars and are receiving dividends and interest of substantial amounts. We are not suggesting, or would want to suggest, that those people should somehow be exempted from paying their taxes on a regular basis.

Private Members' Business
I would suggest that what we try to do is focus on raising the limit and saying only those people who owe tax over $10,000, as opposed to the current $1,000 rule, would have to pay. This would take off the tax rolls for instalment payments 95 per cent of seniors, probably, as well as a certain number of other people who would then simply have to pay at the end of the year when they filed their tax return.
I would invite the member to put forward this suggestion, either in the form that he has it now or in another form depending on how he feels about my comments to the finance committee. I would like to tell him that we intend-the hon. member for Ontario was actually here in the Chamber- to strike a subcommittee shortly in which we want to hear suggestions from members of Parliament and others. The member should pass this idea on to the member for Ontario. We are hopefully going to hold hearings in which we can take ideas like this, examine them carefully and be in a position to make recommendations to the Minister of Finance for his next budget.
We are hoping to commence that process shortly after Thanksgiving. I am hopeful that the member will take the opportunity to pass this suggestion on. Also, I would invite all other hon. members to forward their suggestions on this and other subjects. We are looking for ideas, not ideas that are going to cost the treasury a lot of money, but ideas like this one which do not involve a lot of money. It would relieve the administrative burden for a lot people who are caught in the system inadvertently simply because the rule has been in place for 20 or 30 years without adjustment for inflation. All those people have been brought into the system who were really not intended to be in the system when the rule was first put in place. This would provide fairness for all taxpayers.

Madam Speaker, first of all let me congratulate my colleague from Winnipeg for this exceptional idea. I also thank my colleague from the government side for suggesting that the Tories would at least look at the concept the member has brought forward. I would suggest though that the government member's rationale that a 30 year old might take exception to a 75 year old getting a break that he or
she might not get is the only comment to which I would take exception.
This is an exceptional idea. It is something that has been brought forward to me by many seniors as well. It is an aging population and more and more people will not want to take advantage of this quarterly tax instalment the government has in place.
I wrote to Revenue Canada and asked why it is doing this. The answer was: "We don't necessarily want to do it, but it is Finance that is dictating to us". It said in the statement that the options to seniors are clearly defined in the enclosed instalment guide. I will get to that instalment guide in just a moment to show how clearly defined it is for seniors. I suggest that it is not even clear for an accountant who deals with this each and every day.
When I spoke to a senior official in Finance in Ottawa about this ruling against seniors and self-employed people, he said: "I do not believe this. It is dictatorial. I think seniors should have the choice. I think there is probably a mistake here. I will get back to you".
A week later he said: "I am sorry. I was mistaken. It is Finance. It is income tax legislation. There is nothing we can do about it. I am sorry". The fact that even Finance suggested that it is mean-spirited gives me some hope that the government and the department will take a serious look at a ruling that seniors would say discriminates against them because they are seniors.
Why does the government have to be a financial adviser to a senior citizen? They are suggesting: "Allow me to decide what I will do with my money". The government suggestion is: "We are doing you a favour. We will allow you to pay every three months instead of hitting you hard at the end of the year". However, the seniors are saying: "I do not want that option. Don't do me that favour, please".
The fact is that Revenue Canada will get it out of the senior anyway because it can withhold the GST refund as it so often does. It will hold it against the person for the next five years. There is no danger of Revenue Canada not getting its just desserts. It will get its money one way or another.
September 26, 1991

It was also suggested to me not to worry that seniors would get an invitation. They receive an invitation to get involved in this quarterly instalment. Here is the invitation. Now, I must admit it has been photocopied and it is not in its booklet form. It is a veritable semantic quagmire that defies understanding by anyone, let alone a senior citizen, who reads it. In fact, here is the notice of assessment: "You may be required to pay your taxes for 1990 by quarterly instalments".
As an ex-educator I see the operative word as you "may" be. Not you must or you are obligated to. A senior will read that and say: "Great, I don't have to do this". However, later on they will get hit and they will get hit hard.
These are not necessarily wealthy people. Someone who has a total income of $21,000 a year is not wealthy.
This is from the Declaration of Taxpayers' Rights: "You are entitled to expect that the government will make every reasonable effort to provide you with access to full, accurate and timely information about the Income Tax Act and your rights under it". It says: "You are entitled to an impartial hearing".
I have had seniors come in and say: "I want to protest this". So, I protest on their behalf. Revenue Canada says: "Okay, you may protest and we will hold everything up. But, if the ruling is withheld then the interest will accrue. So you are in big trouble". Wait until I get to the amount of interest charged these seniors when they do not get their quarterly instalment in on time.
Here it is: "A new penalty was introduced in the 1990 taxation year for taxpayers who make late or insufficient instalment payments. A penalty of 50 per cent is charged on the amount by which the instalment interest exceeds the greater or the following amounts". We thought finance companies were mean-spirited.
Here is an example for a senior citizen to follow. "Peter is required to make four instalment payments in 1991 of $1,535 on March 15, June 15, September 15 and December 15. However, he does not make his first payment until March 31", that is 16 days late. "To compensate for making a late payment, Peter pays his June instalment on May 29, rather than on June 15. By
Private Members' Business
paying his June instalment early no instalment interest will be charged when his 1991 return is assessed next year, as long as his remaining payments are paid on time". Do you understand that, Madam Speaker? Nobody understands it.
This is a tip for seniors: "If you realize during the year that your instalments have been less than the required amount"-how would you realize that-"or if one or more of your payments had been late, you can reduce or eliminate an instalment interest charge by overpaying your next payment by paying it early". Again, nobody understands this, let alone a senior.
There is so much here that I am certainly not going to read all of it and I do not want to bore anybody with it. However, it goes on. Near the end of the document, this instalment guide, this invitation says it "uses plain language to explain the common income tax situation". Well, it is not plain language.
I think I am getting away from the principle. We believe that seniors should be given the choice. They should be able to opt out of this wonderful program that Finance has provided them. They should be able to opt out.
Finally: "Improving This Guide: This guide is reviewed each year. If you have any comments or suggestions to improve the explanations provided in this guide, we would like to hear from you". Seniors across this country, and it would appear many of our colleagues, are suggesting to Finance Canada that it should scrap the guide, scrap the quarterly instalments, and give seniors a choice because they want the choice. Surely senior citizens have earned the right to decide when they will pay their taxes. They are not trying to cheat the tax collector. They will pay one way or another, they just want the option.

Madam Speaker, I would just like to make a few comments this afternoon on the motion before the House. I just want to read the motion into the record again:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of changing the collection of income tax as it affects citizens whose income is not taxed at source so that senior citizens who are required to pay income tax in four quarterly instalments will be permitted to pay only one annual instalment.

September 26, 1991
Private Members' Business
I want to commend my colleague from Winnipeg St. James for putting this motion before the House so that several of us can have a chance to comment on it and the House can consider it.
What is the issue at stake? The issue is that seniors no longer holding salaried jobs and who may veiy well be on pensions of some sort, some more than others, are required to pay income tax on a quarterly basis. They must estimate their annual income and determine from that how much they pay every three months.
What is the problem? Well, the problem is that many times they underestimate their payment. They may be late, and, when and if they do, they suffer harsh penalties and terms of interest that are imposed upon them by Revenue Canada.
The facts are that seniors and other individuals owing more than a thousand dollars in tax per year must pay quarterly instalments or pay the price for not doing so. Payment dates must be strictly adhered to and estimates of next year's income must be reliable. Each year, thousands of Canadians make simple errors in calculating what they expect their income to be for the next year, and they may at times miss the date. Yet, the federal government chooses to treat them, for what may be a very innocent mistake, as people who are attempting to defraud the government and punish them with interest charges on these late payments.
Shameful.

On the face of it I admit that quarterly instalments sound like a fair compromise between the majority of people who have their income tax deducted at source and an annual lump sum payment, though we have to take a look at what it does.
Quarterly instalments are meant to act as equalizers to prevent the preferential treatment of one segment of society over another. However, for many members of our society this compromise simply does not work and is not fair.
As I said, often seniors will over-estimate and hence, they can over-pay because they are unable to guess-and that is what it is in many cases-how much their income will be. Interest rates fluctuate up and down. They do not know what their earnings will be for the year so what
is one-quarter of what they are going to make? I remember one gentleman who came in to my office and had sent $350 in every quarter. At the end of the year he got a printout back showing he had paid up in full as of April 30. Then it said that he should have paid by instalment in the previous year. Because he had not, they gave him a warning. In other words, do a better job next year.
As this gentleman said to me, Madam Speaker, he used to have a skylight in the roof of his family room, but after he read that letter, he now has another hole. He said he was absolutely livid after having sent the money based on his calculation, he miscalculated and then was penalized for having done so.
The government suggested the quarterly instalments assist Canadian seniors to avoid budgetary problems. I suggest that these people who have gone through depressions, the Second World War, recessions and are now coping with the government's high level of tax, do not need any lessons in budgeting. If they have problems, heaven help the rest of us.
Seniors are not adolescents needing a guiding hand to learn how to handle their money. They taught us, with the exception of the government that we have at the present time. I am sure they could teach them a few things if only the government would listen.
As my colleague from Winnipeg St. James has said, enough has already been taken away from our seniors. They have had old age security clawback, a changing health care system, caps on funding and other social programs. This government is treating its seniors as if they are a burden, not the asset that they are. Then every three months this government turns around and says: pay up.
Madam Speaker, it would not hurt this House to demonstrate a bit of compassion and understanding and appreciation to the seniors of this country for what they have done during their more active years. I compliment the chairman of the finance committee, the member for Edmonton Northwest from the government benches who just spoke a few minutes ago. As he said, he is chairman of the committee. I compliment him on his suggestion but I point out to him that he is chairman of that committee and I am sure my colleague who spoke earlier this afternoon will give some thought to the suggestion of raising the matter. If we are not going to
September 26, 1991

annual instalments maybe the next best thing we can do is raise the limit somewhat above the $1,000.
Yes, we would be making an exception for one segment of our society, Madam Speaker, but I think we owe it to them. We have an opportunity here in this Parliament to give something back to the seniors in Canada. For once we can do the right thing and make the lives of our senior citizens a little easier. I recommend strongly to the finance committee that it listen to this motion, that it pay attention to this motion, and take some positive steps in that direction.

Madam Speaker, as I rise to speak I think of a certain Manitoba senior who recently said to me: "What is wrong with them in Ottawa? Why don't they listen to us?"
The government may not have been listening, Madam Speaker, but my hon. colleague from Winnipeg St. James is listening. I thank him for his initiative and for giving me the opportunity to speak on this motion.
I read again for the record:
That in the opinion of this House the government should consider the advisability of changing the collection of income tax as it affects senior citizens whose income is not taxed at source so that senior citizens who are required to pay income tax in four quarterly instalments will be permitted to pay only one annual instalment.
In essence, this motion asks this government to allow seniors to pay their income tax in one annual instalment and to be given an exemption if they wish to have one. I listen to the seniors. In fact I say this government better start listening to them.
Seventy years ago, only one in 20 Canadians was over the age of 65. By the year 2021, one of every five Canadians will be a senior. Unlike the stereotype most people have of seniors, they are not feeble and frail. Very few of them are actually frail. Sixty-seven per cent of seniors aged 65 to 74 years say their health is good or excellent.
These people are individuals who have led full lives. They have friends and family. They have grandchildren and hobbies. They like sports and stay tuned to current affairs and politics. They regularly watch us in Parliament, in this House. I am sure many seniors today are watching us as we debate this bill.
Private Members' Business
Many seniors use retirement to go back to school. Unlike in the past when universities and colleges used to be places for the young only, these days every age group in society is represented.
Let us trample the myths that surround old age. These people are busy. They are too busy to be troubled by completing income tax returns every three months. They do not want to be married to a bookkeeper or spend countless evenings calculating estimated earnings. Why can they not pay their taxes once a year? Is it such a difficult wish to grant to our seniors who have helped build this country?
The Manitoba Society of Seniors often helps older men and women who are having trouble doing their taxes. Carol Roberts, Executive Director of the Society says the tax situation is "definitely very frustrating for seniors".
Seniors sometimes have to take money out of the bank early, or lose a month's interest on a bond in order to pay their taxes. At the same time, the Department of Revenue says: "Quarterly income tax payments are easier for seniors because it teaches them how to budget."
I repeat: "it teaches them how to budget." Have you ever heard anything so ridiculous, Madam Speaker? These people made a home in Canada and raised their families. Indeed, they have built this nation, as I said. They saw good times and bad, lean and plenty. Many saved money to see them through their retirement years. Many keep working until their final days, and the government believes that these seniors do not know how to budget.
This to say the least, is insulting. In fact I think seniors could teach the Prime Minister, this government and the Minister of Finance something about budgeting. Ms. Roberts says: "A yearly tax payment will cut down on expenses and worry. It is only common sense."
Where has common sense fled Madam Speaker? It is not only with taxes that seniors are having trouble. They are finding that the government has replaced the mailman with a superbox that sits on the comer, three blocks from their home.
In the winter in Winnipeg North, my constituency, that means three blocks of ice, snow and howling wind between them and a letter from their son or daughter. It

September 26, 1991
Private Members' Business
is three blocks of rain or subzero cold between them and their pension cheque. Little thanks Canada Post, for sacrificing service for profit.
It was not until the government tried to deindex pensions that it felt the full wrath of seniors. I was glad to see that the government had the common sense then to turn and flee from such a foolish plan.
The government now has another splendid opportunity to redeem itself, to cast off its cloak of arrogance and insensitivity. It can demonstrate that it listens to common sense and decency and accept this private members' bill.
Once in awhile there is merit in listening to our seniors. I hope the government will see that. In fact, if the government would listen more it would begin to learn fast because our seniors are trustworthy. They have experience and they have wisdom.
I strongly support this bill of my Liberal colleague, the member for Winnipeg St. James.

Madam Speaker, I rise to participate in the debate on this motion. I do want to thank the hon. member for Winnipeg St. James for bringing it forward. Back in April or May seniors had submitted their tax returns for the 1990 income tax year. They had met their obligations. They put their returns in the mail and, yes, many of them included the amount owing in their return, only, lo and behold, to receive a notice. Whether it be in late April or early May or mid-May, the government said to them: "Yes, we have your cheque. We have the amount. We agree with everything that you have said relative to the tax owing, but there is this problem. You did not pay these quarterly instalments as you should. You did not submit to us 75 per cent of the tax owing on an instalment basis and therefore, although we agree that you paid your tax bill, there is a penalty and there is interest". He and I think most members of the House received those kinds of submissions this spring.
Certainly it was a new submission that I had received. It is not one that I had run into last year or the year before. I am not sure why, but anyway it happened this
year. In that sense I can understand why the member brought forward this kind of presentation.
I should point out that I did have some seniors come into my office. One lady in particular in her late seventies came in with her husband who was in his early eighties. They had the problem that has been described. There was income earned, there was marginal tax paid, and at the end of the year they submitted their returns only to receive this letter that said: "You should have made quarterly instalments".
The question that was asked by this lady who did the return was: "Why was I not told? Why was I not aware that I had to make these instalments?" I mentioned to her that one of the things the government does annually-there are a number of documents, I think some of which were referenced by one of the other members who spoke- is to include in one of the OAS payments that is made by the Government of Canada a notice about the quarterly instalment requirements and how it is possible for a senior, in fact for anyone receiving government cheques, to create a deduction process so that they can make not only quarterly instalments but monthly if they prefer.
The lady mentioned to me: "Well, gee, I guess there should be more emphasis on that because I would like to take advantage of those quarterly instalments. I would like to because I find it difficult to write a cheque for $2,800 at the end of the year. We prefer to pay $700 a quarter". Yes, it is budgeting, and I can certainly understand comments from one of the members from Winnipeg that seniors certainly know how to budget. Nobody is debating that. They do, but some do have difficulty as I am sure all members in this House will agree, making ends meet. There is just not enough money to go around for all the things that they feel they need or would like to do.
Sometimes if you only have to make that quarterly payment there is a tendency to borrow that $10 from that bank account and replace it next month or the month after. Well next month comes and you do not replace it, and particularly for seniors it becomes very difficult. I understand what some of the members have said, that seniors pride themselves in paying their bills. You can just see it when the tax bill is due in a municipality. Who
September 26, 1991

are the people who are lined up to make sure that they pay that bill on time? Senior citizens.
It is a problem if you allow them to make one payment a year. Some of them do prefer to have that option of making those quarterly instalments.
In this motion the member has put forward, nothing prevents that from happening if a senior wanted to make those quarterly instalments.
I come to the other side of this equation, quarterly instalments for simply a blanket suggestion of seniors, and there are very few seniors who fit into this category. Imagine a circumstance, as was described by several speakers, in which people receive the Canada Savings Bonds interest in October or November, but they really have to pay the taxes six months before, in March. Not just Canada Savings Bonds, there are many seniors who have registered retirement income plans that pay out toward the end of the year, or savings certificates at banks. Interest payments are like that.
Imagine another circumstance. For example, the Bronfmans are shareholders in large corporations and those corporations might only pay dividends in December. I do not know what the income of the Bronfmans is, but it is certainly substantial.
Imagine saying to them: "We realize you have a million dollars in dividends this year, which you got paid in December, but it is okay, you do not have to make any quarterly instalments on that kind of income".
I can tell you that members opposite and members on this side, I for one, would be rather upset to think of people like the Bronfmans, the McCains, the Irvings, the Reichmans only making payments once a year. I have great difficulty with that. That is why I have some difficulty with the concept of the motion the way it is presented.
We heard the hon. member for Edmonton Northwest talk about a proposal within the finance committee. I can tell you that when I started to receive these calls back in April, when we were setting up the agenda of the finance committee, that was one of the very clear suggestions I made. We should review a number of tax proposals that do not necessarily cost the government less revenue or more revenue. The way they are structured is not working.
I had this one in mind and a number of others. The committee agreed, with the support of all members of
Private Members' Business
the committee, Liberal, NDP and Conservative members, that there are some tax things we ought to look at.
I can tell the hon. member that in support of what the member for Edmonton Northwest indicated, the committee will be receiving submissions and we hope to start our work on this subject and others that relate very closely to this within about the next three weeks, with the aim of producing a report with specific recommendations.
I guess I would comment that although I do not necessarily support this motion the way it is written, I do support the idea that there ought to be a group of people, seniors and others, who are on that very low threshold of income. Those who have to pay more than $1,000 a year of income tax should be given the option of only paying their tax once a year. They can choose that option. For that lady who came into my office who would prefer a quarterly system, I certainly would not want to deny that option to her if that is what she prefers.
I think there should be a mechanism in place whereby some people can make their tax payments once a year and that should be at income tax time, the end of March. I think there is a threshold that I am sure we in this House can come to that would be acceptable, so that a lot of seniors would not be faced with the challenge.
What is that threshold? I am not sure. I use the names of maybe four families whose names are well-known. I do not know how much they make. We can all only speculate on that matter. I guess what I am saying is that I do not think these kinds of things should be blanket rules for all people. There are a number of senior citizens who are still working. Seniors beyond age 65 who are gainfully employed on a monthly basis and receive cheques have to have their income tax deducted at source.
There are some seniors who have one method of income who have to pay monthly or bi-weekly, or however they are paid, and you would establish another rule for other seniors who receive their income in a different fashion.
I like the idea of what is being presented by the member. I can say that as a member of the finance committee we have discussed this in a preliminary stage. Our workload has not permitted us to get on to the subject yet. Even yesterday we had a discussion on the subject and said: "Okay, we want to get going on some of these other issues".

Adjournment Debate
There are a couple of other things on the finance committee agenda, but we are within the next week hopefully going to release a request for members of Parliament to deal with this kind of tax suggestion. I suspect in our work with our constituencies we know of a number of these kinds of things, where for a very minor change we would satisfy an avTul lot of people. It would not cost the Government of Canada really any money or any lost revenue, but it would be a very positive thing to do to make the system of taxation in this country as fair as possible to as many people as possible, if it is possible to have taxation fair.
Nobody likes to pay taxes. We all recognize that there are a lot of things we get from government that have to be paid for. People are willing to pay their share, but let us make it so that some people who find it a little more difficult to pay their share on a monthly or quarterly basis have an easier way to do it. I look forward to that debate in the finance committee.

Madam Speaker, I want to take up a question that I raised March 31, 1991 with respect to international trade, specifically as it was impacted by the free trade agreement.
I was very specific on that day inasmuch as I asked the Minister of Finance to take a close look at the way that Customs officials on the American side of the border were monitoring Canadian products going into the American market. They were doing it with a severity that was being harmful to our own products moving south. At the same time Canadian Customs officials were being a
little bit more generous in the way that they were applying Canadian Customs regulations on products of American origin.
The Minister of Finance at the time gave me an indication that he would look into the matter. When I gave him very specific items of indication, especially relative to the printing industry and the impact on 70,000 employees of the printing industry, the minister at the time said that he would look into it with more precision and would get back to me.
Today is September 26. In the meantime, what we have seen is that there has not been any effort to level the playing field. The free trade agreement was supposed to level the playing field between Canadian and American marketplaces, between Canadian producers and American producers. We were going to open up the markets on one side and on the other. No such thing has happened.
I pointed out on March 31, and I gave very specific examples, that American clients of Canadian producers were actually closing accounts because the consumers in the United States were rejecting products marked "made in Canada". I find that absolutely shameful.
The tardiness of the minister's response is absolutely inexcusable. It is absolutely inexcusable because we have had a series of studies that have been produced since then that have indicated the impact of the free trade agreement on Canadian jobs and on Canadian manufacturers.
For example, one study gave us an indication that 315,000 manufacturing jobs in the first 29 months of the post-free trade agreement were lost, most of them from the province of Ontario. They moved south. There is a sorry admission by the senior advisory to the then Minister of Finance: "The problem now is that we are losing manufacturing activity itself to the United States and that once these jobs go outside Canada they aren't coming back". He preferred to remain anonymous for understandable reasons.
Not only are we losing trade, we are actually losing our ability to produce products so that we can generate trade. The main reason for it again is because what is happening is that the states bordering on Canada are engaging in a very competitive, aggressive, and I might say perhaps not totally ethical, attack on our manufacturing sector.
September 26, 1991

The Canadian Manufacturers' Association last spring surveyed some 635 members and 237 of them concluded that it would be cheaper to operate in the U.S., in states bordering on Canada. Some 156 of them had been approached by state governments to relocate south. The incentives are lower taxes, lower land costs, lower operating costs, and other kinds of subsidies that we cannot offer. Those kinds of subsidies were not supposed to be a part of the free trade agreement.
I was looking forward to getting a response from the Minister of Finance to give Canadians an explanation as to why we would tolerate those kinds of practices south of the border that drain away our manufacturing sector but we cannot do the same thing here.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Plourde (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of International TVade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to provide some clarification in response to the question raised by the hon. member for Eglinton-Lawrence regarding U.S. requirements for country of origin markings which have raised concerns in the Canadian printing industry.
According to the U.S. Tariff Act of 1930, all foreign goods imported into the United States must show the country of origin in a readily visible location and in as legible, indelible and permanent a manner as the nature of the item allows. The U.S. Congress wanted the ultimate purchaser to be able to know the country of origin upon inspection of the item, before he decides whether or not to buy it.
Madam Speaker, the government understands the concerns of the Canadian printing industry. During the free trade talks with the United States, we tried to reach an agreement on eliminating these requirements for Canadian goods.
The U.S. government refused to consider substantial changes in its marking regulations. We intend to raise the matter again with the United States and Mexico during the trilateral talks on North American free trade. We will make every effort to have these requirements eliminated for goods originating in Canada, but we are not very clear as to what kind of measures will be accepted during these talks.
Adjournment Debate
We also raised the matter with GATT in the Uruguay Round. Madam Speaker, the hon. member also raised the question of Canadian marking regulations. This is a matter for the Minister of National Revenue, but I can inform the hon. member that the hon. Otto Jelinek recently wrote to the president of the Canadian Printing Industries Association, giving the assurance that customs officials at Revenue Canada were reviewing the administration of the regulations on marking of imported goods to guarantee that the regulations are administered according to the same rules and in the same spirit.

Madam Speaker, earlier, on September 23, I asked a question in this House about the notorious COSICS contract.
Let me refresh the memory of the House as to what we are talking about. In the summer of 1987 three bids were entered on the COSICS computer contract for External Affairs. Fenco-Lavelin was one of them, SHL Systemhouse was one, and DMR was the other.
In October 1987 the bidders were advised that there would be a bid recall and to re-submit bids by January
1988.	Unfortunately the bids apparently were visible from one bidder to the other, which means that the bidder who had the least advantage was able to find information to enhance the bid.
Be that as it may, there were three bidders-the same ones again-in January 1988. After the bidding process was over, the losing bidders alleged that there was bid rigging in the process and the RCMP was invited to investigate the situation.
With regard to another related inquiry, an alleged sting operation against a member of the other place, the Marin commission of inquiry heard testimony from one of the losing bidders, a Mr. Ducros, who said that he had lunch in a Montreal restaurant with, and I will read it from the transcript: "Senator Michel Cogger" and another Senator, and that name is blanked out. The name is on the court document that I have in hand. It is blanked out. The only thing that we know is that the last letter is "u."

Adjournment Debate
There have been numerous similar allegations with regard to this bid. There have been cost overruns of a magnitude which is unbelievable. We have now heard, in an interview that the Minister of Supply and Services gave earlier this week, that the whole system, after spending some $53 million for the first phase, not only does not work but will not work. The only thing it will do is connect Ottawa and Washington. To connect Ottawa and Washington all we need to do is put someone with a briefcase on a plane three times a day.

We don't need to spend $53 million and have all this scandal, and then be denied information. I am very anxious to know the answer. Who is this person with eleven letters in his name, the last one a "u"?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Department of Supply and Services, on behalf of the Department of External Affairs, signed a contract to acquire a Canadian on-line secure information and communications system.
To date, the Department of External Affairs has spent $53 million, not $140 million, of a budget totalling $56 million for the first phase of COSICS, a new secure telecommunications system to replace the old system that the department uses throughout the world on behalf of all departments.
Therefore, Phase I of COSICS is within the budget allocated by the Treasury Board ministers in 1987. The project is two years late. This is not an excuse, I agree, but it is one of the most complex and important data transmission projects ever undertaken in Canada. Phase I of COSICS is operational; since late 1989, it has become the mainstay of our North American secure communications system, with 1,100 daily users. Now that system installation is complete, we expect final approval of system security by the end of the year.
Madam Speaker, the department has not stopped the project, on the contrary. This project was designed in two phases, precisely for the purpose of checking system reliability. The rapid progress of technology in this field since 1987 well shows the wisdom of this approach, and the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell will surely agree with me. The department is using personal
computers to make up for lost time and to complete the project within the limit set by the 1987 budget.
Madam Speaker, I will certainly not answer speculative questions about a twelve-letter name supposedly on a document we have not seen that the hon. member says he has. I have no information and it is not for me to play that role. Let the court do its job, Madam Speaker!

Madam Speaker, I rise this evening, as I have done repeatedly in this House this year and last year, in what is so far a futile attempt to convince this government that there is a crisis facing the port of Halifax.
The latest occasion was Thursday of last week when I asked the Prime Minister about a report that had been initiated by Ports Canada and that we understand to be completed but that was not going to be made public, was not going to be given to members of Parliament for the city of Halifax, the city of Dartmouth, and in Nova Scotia generally. I asked whether the Prime Minister had any words which could lead us to believe that there was an interest in saving one of the great ports of this country which is in clear and desperate distress.
The response, I am afraid, was again evasion. It is my submission that this government must act now to stop the decline into obscurity of what has historically been Canada's greatest port. It is not as though we are asking for a handout.
Halifax has managed to get by with a great deal less assistance than Some of our competitors. We do not mind that. We are not complaining but we do note that there are virtually free ice-breaking and pilotage fees for the port of Montreal. We note also that there have been MIL bailouts in the order of $350 million.
I note most particularly, as I have noted before, that there was a decision by the Government of Canada to assist CP Rail in the purchase of the Delaware and Hudson railway. This is a thorn in the side of Haligonians, and Nova Scotians generally.
This railway is now drawing business away from the port of Halifax. It is drawing it in great numbers, to the direct advantage of the port of New York.
September 26, 1991

This government speaks of competitiveness, presumably in an effort to rationalize our practices with those of the United States. That is fine, too. The port of Halifax has been and can be competitive if the government does not close it down as a result of its policy.
The Americans, for example, have invested $750 million to upgrade the ports of New York and Baltimore. What kind of environment is that subsidy to those ports going to create for Halifax? What is it going to do to Saint John? What is it going to do to Montreal?
Given the government's silence on this matter, apparently the government believes that the ramifications will not make much difference. I can tell you, Madam Speaker, they will, they do, and they have.
When will the government open its eyes to the fact that CN Rail is currently uncompetitive, grotesquely so? It is uncompetitive because of the National Transportation Act, because it took CN eight years to wake up to the fact that its rail rates were too high, and because the government taxes the railway far more than its American competitors are taxed.
We need the federal government to help us create the famous and oft talked about level playing field. Make CN Rail competitive. Lessen the tax burden, both on the port and on the vital infrastructure surrounding it.
If the government gives Halifax a fighting chance instead of subsidizing its competitors, then we in Halifax can do what we have always done best. We in Halifax want the chance to do what we have always done best. What is that?
It is to move the world's goods through our port, the port of Halifax, the port that is the best in the world if we only have the chance to show it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think we have answered the question on numerous occasions for the member.
Whether she cares to admit it the difficulty facing the port of Halifax is the product of a highly competitive global trading environment that all our ports are facing.
It is time that everyone who is concerned about Halifax started to work together. It is clear that we on
Adjournment Debate
this side of the House are doing so. As the Prime Minister told the hon. member last week, he met with the premier of Nova Scotia, who brought constructive and thoughtful proposals for the benefit of the Halifax harbour.
In addition, both the Canada Ports Corporation and CN have been working very hard to increase their marketing competitiveness. CN has firmly committed itself to the Halifax route and it is presently leasing double-stacked cars to service containerized freight traffic.
In addition, the railway is increasing the overhead clearances of the Halifax-Moncton portion of the CN main line. The provincial government of Nova Scotia has committed up to $11.1 million to acquire modem, double-stacked rail cars.
My hon. friend opposite in her question mentioned a specific report concerning competitiveness. As I understand it, the Ports Corporation conducted an analysis of the container situation. The Ports Corporation has made the decision not to release the report.
Instead, it is confident that what is more important for the port of Halifax is that it has undertaken an exhaustive program of consultations with the groups that have an interest and a role to play in the continuing viability of this great port.
I would like the House to know, for the record, that none of us is in the least bit complacent about the problems facing the port of Halifax. Nevertheless, it would be more useful to extol the virtues of this port rather than focusing on the negative at every opportunity-
The member could perhaps also admit that even with today's problems, the port output is still well above what it was five years ago. Indeed, since 1984, according to the Halifax Port Corporation, the port experienced continuous growth until this year.
I can assure the member, as the right hon. Prime Minister said, that this government will be working in partnership with the provincial government, the railway and the port officials for Halifax's future prosperity.

Adjournment Debate RIGHTS OF THE CHILD

Madam Speaker, this government, to the embarrassment of all Canadians, is refusing to ratify the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.
Madam Speaker, as you know, we are signatories of this document. Our very own Prime Minister co-chaired the conference which produced the convention, yet he and his government steadfastly refuse to ratify it. I do not think that this is acceptable.
However, I believe I know why this is happening. Part of the convention reads:
Any child that is deprived of liberty shall be held separate and apart
from adults unless it is not in the interests of that child to do so.
These few lines are very progressive. It is a valuable document and our government, by not ratifying it, is preventing much needed protection for children. Why? Because these words stand in contrast to the government's own policy of transferring young offenders to adult prisons to serve their sentences.
There is a very great concern out there, particularly in the large cities, about young offenders and the fact that these young offenders are committing so many crimes and are back out on the street in a short period of time. However, what the people do not realize is that the problem with young offenders originates with the government and its policies, that the government incarcerates young offenders with adult criminals where they are assaulted physically and sexually, learn more about crime and how to commit it and are back out on the street in a relatively short period of time without any kind of rehabilitation.
This is wrong. Certainly the young offenders should be incarcerated until they have the proper rehabilitation and assistance. This may mean longer periods of time. Certainly that is acceptable. But what is not acceptable is to put young people out on the street again without proper assistance. To incarcerate them with adults is only exacerbating the problem and making these young people, when they get out of incarceration, more susceptible to committing other crimes.
It is being done because building youth detention facilities is not a politically positive move. It reflects, in all of us, the shortcomings of we as human beings, but it is necessary to have a youth program that is going to serve the needs of that youth. The problems of violence
in our cities is now rampant. We have to look at it realistically. We have to ratify this agreement and government has to look at this question.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of TVansport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the question of the hon. member with respect to the ratification of the Convention on the Rights of the Child.
As you all know, the convention came into force on September 2,1990. Canada had signed the convention on May 28, 1990.
The Department of Justice has co-ordinated the review of federal legislation and policies in light of the convention. We are proud to underline the fact that Canadian legislation and policies dealing with children's rights are progressive and go far beyond the objectives of the convention.
With respect to the specific issue of the detention of children, the convention provides that a child deprived of liberty shall be separated from adults unless it is in his or her best interests not to do so. Although we are in agreement with this principle, we consider that it is necessary to enter a reservation. There are two reasons for that reservation.
The first one is that we must be able to take into account other relevant considerations, such as the wellbeing of other children kept in custody or the safety of the public.
The second one is that we are currently in the process of consulting with the provinces and the territories on the issue of the appropriate placement of young offenders.
We need time to complete this process in a responsible fashion. We are trying to develop a response which is the most appropriate, taking into account all of the circumstances of young offenders who have been transferred to the adult court and other young offenders.
The hon. member has suggested that the situation of young offenders being held in custody is going to be made worse by Bill C-12, an act to amend the Young Offenders Act and the Criminal Code, which is presently before the House of Commons. He refers to the proposed amendment to test for the transfer of a young offender to the adult court but which retains the principle of the interest of society and specifies that this

principle includes the objective of affording protection to the public and to the rehabilitation of the young person.
The objective of the federal government is to ensure that the best possible decision can be made at a transfer hearing in the interest of both the youth before the court and of the public. The proposed test is not advanced to secure more transfers, and transfer as an option is intended to remain an exceptional procedure.
Given the range of interpretation to date on the current test, it was viewed as highly desirable to lessen the unequal application of the test and to reinforce the notion that both the needs of the youth and the protection of the public are primary considerations.
It is our understanding that all provinces and territories support ratifications of this important convention and we are working together to promote and improve the situation of young offenders kept in custody. The reservation would permit us to ratify the convention before the end of the year, before awaiting the completion of the federal-provincial-territorial consultation.

Madam Speaker, last week in this House I raised the matter of issuing false passports, as did the leader of my party, and as did the member for Scarborough West, our immigration critic. Since then I have been increasingly concerned by the attitude displayed by this government and the response received.
When I travel to other countries, I am treated very well, thanks to my Canadian passport. When my constituents become Canadian citizens, they are amazed at the respect the Canadian passport garners them at border points where before they had been less than welcome.
Will this continue? Will Canadians still be so welcome when the international community hears that this government will issue a false passport in three days if you go in person and in two weeks if you use the mail-in program?
The minister responsible said, and I quote: "Security is our highest priority in the issuing of passports".
I did some checking and security is not exactly air tight in the passport office. I was shocked to find that the guarantors are checked at random. In my career as principal and as member of Parliament, I have signed
Adjournment Debate
dozens of forms as guarantor. In over 30 years I only had two calls to check, to verify whether I knew the applicant applying for the passport.
When the guarantors are checked, after the passport is issued, how does the minister propose to get the documents back after the fact, particularly since the fraudulent passport was probably mailed to a false address?
I was also shocked at the ease with which birth certificates can be forged, sometimes with as little as a bottle of white-out and a photocopier. Clearly, there must be more stringent measures adopted.
I call on this government to immediately develop national standards for birth certificates, standards which are the same for all provinces. Huge amounts of money are spent in the printing process to ensure that Canadian passports cannot be forged. In relative terms precious little time is spent to ensure that the passports are not issued based on false documentation.
I call on this government to use the $5 million surplus in the passport revolving fund to hire enough people to call every guarantor personally on the telephone. Sometimes a constituent comes to my office asking for help getting some kind of a travel document while they are waiting for landed immigrant status in Canada. I cannot say how many times I have been asked: "Are you asking us to push this case without the proper security checks? Are you asking us to compromise the integrity of the Canadian travel document?"
No. I am asking that the integrity of Canada and of the Canadian passport be upheld at all costs. As a Canadian citizen, I expect this government to do something about the situation. I expect that only Canadian citizens will have our passport. Not spies, not criminals, not drug lords, not people whose only claim to our passports is that they are rich enough to be able to afford the $20,000 to $50,000 currently being charged on the black market for this document.
In closing, the Secretary of State for External Affairs says that she has asked her department to investigate and make a full report. I ask the parliamentary secretary if the minister will table that report in this House and when?
As well, will she assure this House that her minister will table one accurate report rather than the three or four versions she issued in the A1 Mashat report?

September 26, 1991
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mrs. Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on September 19, the hon. member for Park-dale-High Park asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs about reports in the newspapers pertaining to the issuance of fraudulent passports.
Internationally, the Canadian passport is reputed to be one of the most secure travel documents. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs pointed out, we are taking very seriously the matter of security as it affects the issuance of passports. The Passport Office works very closely with the RCMP to ensure the integrity of our travel documents.
I may point out that the procedures and technology we use are constantly being evaluated to respond to these challenges. No system, whatever security measures are taken, is entirely safe from fraud and false statements.
Hon. members should realize we must strike a balance between increased security and our ability to provide an efficient service at reasonable cost. It has always been our objective to maintain the right balance.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has indicated that departmental officials will be drafting recommendations for improving passport security. We believe that such measures could be implemented at relatively low cost, with as little inconvenience as possible to the Canadian public.
Madam Speaker, in concluding, I hope that my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, will consider the positive recommendations made by the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park.
